nytimes.com.title: Kenya Records Ebola Case for First Time
nytimes.com.text:
Kenya has recorded its first case of Ebola after the virus was diagnosed in a man who had arrived from the Democratic Republic of Congo, the government announced on Tuesday.
Congo has suffered a severe outbreak of Ebola, the second-largest on record, after cases began spreading, as early as January. More than 4,000 people have died of Ebola in the country since May, according to official figures.
The case in Kenya, found in a man who died on Monday in a private hospital in the capital, raised concern of a cross-border spread, though public health officials said that single cases could quickly be contained as long as the right measures were followed.
The man, a Kenyan citizen who had lived in Congo for seven years, became ill a month ago and had been treated at hospitals in Congo, the Kenyan cabinet secretary for health, Aden Duale, told a news conference. The authorities did not name the man.
The man had traveled by road to Uganda and then took a flight to Nairobi, the Kenyan capital, on Saturday, Mr. Duale said.
After passing through health and immigration controls at the airport, the man was driven directly by a relative and friend in a private vehicle to a hospital in Nairobi “where he was quickly isolated in a separate room,” Mr. Duale noted. Doctors identified Ebola symptoms and, given that he had arrived from Congo, the man was tested and found positive for the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, Mr. Duale added. The man was later transferred to an isolation unit.

nytimes.com.title: The Separatist Parti Québécois Wins Quebec Election, Reviving Sovereignty Push
nytimes.com.text:
The separatist Parti Québécois won the provincial election in Quebec on Monday, possibly setting the stage for a referendum on the French-speaking province’s independence from Canada in the next few years.
Voters hungry for change returned the Parti Québécois to power for the first time in 12 years, even though they displayed little interest in the commitment of its leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, to hold a referendum on secession from Canada.
The Parti Québécois fell short of clinching a majority, winning 59 seats out of 127 in the provincial legislature, according to incomplete results late Monday. That could make it difficult for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon to fulfill his campaign promise to hold a referendum after President Trump leaves office in 2029 and the economy stabilizes.
A Parti Québécois minority government could struggle to stay in power for a full four-year term. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon will also govern after winning only about 28 percent of the popular vote, according to incomplete results, making it hard for him to claim a popular mandate.
“A referendum is an opportunity to decide for yourself,” Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. “It’s an act of democracy. It’s up to no one but us, as a people, to determine our national future.”
But in an acknowledgment of his government’s minority status, he said he would call a referendum “hopefully, with the help of other pro-independence lawmakers from other parties.”

nytimes.com.title: Germany’s Far Right Claims Its First Statehouse Speaker Since 1945
nytimes.com.text:
A normally ho-hum procedural vote in a small state will be closely watched across Germany on Tuesday, when a far-right politician is expected to be elected to lead a state Parliament for the first time since the Nazi era.
In the legislative election last month in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, the Alternative for Germany party, labeled “suspected extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence service, won 39 of 83 seats. The party, known by its German initials AfD, far outperformed every other party, delivering a shock to the country’s postwar consensus.
The next step toward taking power is expected on Tuesday, when lawmakers will be sworn in and could elect the AfD’s Tobias Rausch as president of the Parliament. In that role, Mr. Rausch, 35, would preside over the legislative agenda, parliamentary bureaucracy and ceremonial roles, like hosting memorials commemorating the Holocaust.
A higher, more important hurdle awaits in December, when the state Parliament is expected to fill the most powerful state position, minister president — the equivalent of governor, with control of the executive branch. It is unclear if the AfD’s candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, can win that vote; until then Sven Schulze of the Christian Democrats remains acting governor of Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany’s least populous states, with about 2.1 million people.
What would the AfD do in power?
The party has made it clear that it does not intend to allow business as usual.
The AfD successfully ran on an anti-immigration, anti-establishment campaign, pro-fossil fuel campaign, but such issues are decided on the federal level, beyond the reach of a state government. At the state level, it plans to focus on education and culture issues.
During the campaign, Mr. Siegmund vowed to segregate schools, separating the children of asylum seekers from other students, and to replace all rainbow flags in schools with German flags. The party has called for more patriotic arts from institutions that rely on state funding.

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: At Starbucks, the future is smaller
cnn.com.text: Starbucks is on a mission to recapture its roots as a place to sit down for a cup of coffee. But it doesn’t think it needs a big footprint to deliver on that promise. A new café prototype that opened last month in San Antonio has all the features of a typical Starbucks, like plush seating, bakery treats displayed in a glass case as well as an espresso bar for baristas to make drinks. However, it’s a fraction of the size of a usual location. The new design helps Starbucks push into areas where real estate is expensive, particularly in major cities. Starbucks reworked the counter with a new “folded bar” configuration to fit into narrower spaces rather than running the entirety of a café. But the chain said the new format still has seating for people to socialize and connect, which has become a hallmark of its reinvigoration plan to recapture the “third place” energy that’s a priority for CEO Brian Niccol. “These particular new formats are really stretching us to be more adaptable to different types of location, different shapes and different sizes, but they still hold all of the aspects of the (coffee house) experience,” said Dawn Clark, the company’s senior vice president of global concepts and design. Prior to Niccol’s arrival in 2024, Starbucks largely tailored its locations to customers picking up orders off its mobile app. It pulled out 30,000 comfortable seats, installed hard wooden stools and blocked electrical outlets, making cafes a less desirable place to hang out. Sales suffered as a result, as well as for a variety of other reasons, including higher prices, longer waits for pickup orders and lackluster food options. In 2025, as part of a $1 billion restructuring effort, the chain announced a massive renovation plan that brought back cozy seating, more plugs and free refills to encourage customers to stick around. So far, 1,500 existing locations have been redesigned in North America, with Starbucks planning to accelerate the face lifts. A smaller-sized prototype could fit into its growth plans. Smaller size Starbucks is applying aspects of its broader redesign project to this smaller prototype. It doesn’t want repeat the mistakes of the ill-fated pick-up only stores that were created for small spaces. Niccol shuttered them in July 2025, saying the locations were “overly transactional.” The sterile design didn’t have seats and encouraged people to order strictly via its mobile app. Clark used that as a case study for this design so as to not limit how people order their drinks. About 30% of customers use mobile ordering, the company says. “Customers have variable needs and they would like to be able to choose different ways of interacting with us, depending on what their day is like,” she told CNN, adding that the new locations let people order in person, for delivery, on the app and even at a drive-thru. So far, six locations of the smaller prototype are open, including in San Antonio and Manhattan. The company declined to reveal the square footage of the new design. Starbucks’ success Starbucks has had a mixed success in attracting people back to the chain. The company has closed hundreds of locations over the past two years across North America. However, same-store US sales turned positive in the most recent quarter, and it has plans to open about 5,000 new locations in the coming years. Clark said they’ve learned from the 1,000 locations they’ve remolded so far, and plan to use the information from both customers and employees in this new, smaller design. “It’s very symbiotic and we’re getting a lot of feedback that the kind of reenergizing of the coffee house is really positive for both sides.”

cnn.com.title: Trump draws backlash after he suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
cnn.com.text: Officials in California denounced comments made by President Donald Trump as “dangerous” on Monday after he appeared to suggest Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego – major cities in a state he has often criticized. Trump was speaking at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, ahead of the midterm elections and said he wanted to see “a tremendous victory because it verifies all the things we did.” The president called the war with Iran a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” adding that Iran could take out a city. “Let, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s this is a very small price to pay and it’s gonna be over with very soon,” Trump said in comments that drew swift backlash from California’s leaders. CNN has reached out to the White House for more information on what Trump meant by his comments about the two cities. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom called the president “deranged and dangerous,” while Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the statements against the city “could potentially compromise our safety.” “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” said Bass, also a Democrat. The Democratic mayor of San Diego, Todd Gloria, said the city “is not collateral damage. We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” Trump’s comments also drew criticism from Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond, who said he “vehemently” disagreed with the president. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” said Desmond, who is running in California’s 48th Congressional district. He added, “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” Trump’s highlighting of cities in California that could be targeted by Iran comes as he has frequently criticized the state and its leaders over immigration, state elections and wildfires. The president also said during his speech in Nebraska that the war is “going to end very soon.” At the onset of the war, Trump had vowed that the conflict would only last a few weeks, but it has since gone on seven months. The president made the new argument last week that his initial four- to six-week timeline had just been about the time it would take to eradicate the nuclear threat from Iran and not the time it would take to conclude the entire war. CNN’s Kaanita Iyer contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Buttigieg, Gallego and other potential 2028 Democratic contenders set to discuss party’s future at post-midterms meeting
cnn.com.text: A group of potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidates is heading to Denver days after the midterms to discuss the party’s future, in one of the party’s first major gatherings following the election. Attendees will include former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and former US Ambassador to Japan Rahm Emanuel, as well as Sens. Ruben Gallego of Arizona, Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, according to an initial lineup shared first with CNN. The group of speakers also includes Govs. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, plus several additional members of Congress. The “What’s Next” summit is being hosted from November 12-14 by Majority Democrats, an organization that launched last year to help Democrats win in more places. In staging the event less than two weeks after the midterms, where Democrats hope to retake the Senate and the House, the group is looking to move quickly to outline the lessons learned from the election that could be instructive going forward, including in the next White House race. “This isn’t a policy conference nor a talk shop on tactics,” Rep. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, said in a statement. “What’s Next is timed for a unique moment after the midterms and before the presidential to debate a vision for the Democratic Party. Politicians who believe they have that vision should be on that stage.” Organizers chose Denver partly because it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. The initial lineup also includes top party strategists such as David Axelrod, former senior adviser to President Barack Obama and a chief political analyst at CNN; Quentin Fulks, former principal deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris in 2024; and Morris Katz, adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Majority Democrats is not the only organization holding an event in the immediate aftermath of the midterms in a bid to shape the party’s future. Two days after the election, some of the party’s most prominent strategists and commentators are set to converge in Washington, DC, for Crooked Con, which is hosted by the progressive media company Crooked Media.

cnn.com.title: Disney increases park prices every year. Here’s how it avoids pricing out families
cnn.com.text: Disney raised prices on many of its theme park offerings today, coinciding with the start of the company’s new fiscal year. But consumers aren’t pushing back the way they did a few years ago. Disney’s price hikes are an annual October ritual for the company, and it’s always a tricky balancing act between increasing revenue and consumers’ willingness to pay. Many ticket types, passes and add-ons at Disneyland are not increasing at all this time. But premium products are getting more expensive, like the highest-level, skip-the-line service at Walt Disney World, which could now run just shy of the $500 mark during peak demand. It’s a reflection of the company’s strategy: Spread the price boosts across different audiences, while leaving bottom-tier prices - like the slowest season, one-day, one-park tickets - unchanged. Its theme parks strategy, Disney said, has evolved over time. Higher-priced premium products and add-ons, alongside targeted discounts and a refresh of older attractions, allowed the company this summer to generate the strongest parks and cruises revenue in two years. The company kept entry-level prices stable this year, when many consumers are reigning in discretionary spending. “Our goal is to put guests at the center of our decision making, and that starts by listening to them,” Thomas Mazloum, chairman of Disney Experiences, told CNN ahead of the price hikes. “That matters more now when families are watching every dollar, and we see it in the choices they make every day — in how they plan, in how far ahead.” Disneyland holds relatively steady Some prices at Disneyland are inching up, like adding the option to hop between two parks in the same day ($5 to $15 more), most middle-tier Disneyland tickets (about $5 or 3% more), and its Lightning Lane Multi Pass skip-the-line service ($1 or 3% more). However, a broad slate of products at Disneyland are not increasing in price: the cheapest tickets for the slowest days of the year, the peak tickets for the busiest days of the year, multi-day tickets, parking and annual passes. The base ticket price has held steady at $104 since 2019. But for the first time in a decade, the most expensive one-day, one-park ticket for Disneyland (usually during end-of-year holidays) is also not budging from its current $224. The fact that none of the annual passes are changing in price is also a first. The relative lack of price movement this year in Anaheim, California, speaks to the main clientele: locals. Disney told CNN that visitation to Disneyland tends to be more regional with shorter stays; Disney World guests typically plan further ahead, travel longer distances, and take longer vacations. Pnina Feldman, associate professor of technology and operations management at the University of Virginia, said Californians “are deciding how many times to visit this year.” “That decision is price sensitive,” she said. Different coasts, different needs The very same items at Disney World in Florida are seeing different price treatments. “We have all kinds of guests coming through our gates,” Disney’s Mazloum said, “and it’s exactly why we think about pricing market by market, rather than with one broad brush.” Current Disney World ticket prices have been set through October 2027. But for the remainder of 2027, the new price of the peak, one-day, one-park ticket will increase by $10 to $229 plus tax. The lowest-priced, one-day, one-park ticket will stay the same at $119 plus tax. Feldman said that at Disney World, more guests are from out of state. “For guests who flew in and booked a hotel, a few dollars on a ticket rarely changes the decision to go, so the increase in price won’t fundamentally decrease demand,” she said. Annual passes to Disney World are going up by $10 to $120, depending on the pass. Middle-tier Disney World tickets, multi-day tickets, and a skip-the-line service for individual premium rides, will also see a moderate increase. The high-end version of that service that allows guests into every available fast lane without reservations could go up $50 based on demand. The price of the cheaper skip-the-line option that requires reservations, as well as parking rates, will not change. Listening to feedback Gavin Doyle, founder of third-party Disney news site MickeyVisit.com, said his readers follow the company — and the annual price increases — closely. “I’m just seeing Disney start to really listen to fan feedback in a way that they haven’t in the past, always,” Doyle said. In post-pandemic years, he said some guests felt like the changes to policies and price increases made it more difficult to visit a place over which they feel so much ownership. In response, Disney rolled back some pandemic-era decisions, such as making Disney World hotel parking free again for guests. Beci Mahnken, CEO of MEI-Travel agency, said that even in financially uncertain times, her clients aren’t foregoing Disney trips altogether. However, “some clients are willing to adjust their dates, resort or length of stay when the right offer comes along because it can make a meaningful difference in the overall cost,” Mahnken said. That’s exactly what Disney is hoping for: to use pricing to spread crowds out more evenly throughout the year, hopefully providing a better experience for all visitors. “We’re so proud that guests keep choosing us, year after year. It tells us we’re getting that balance right,” Mazloum said.

cnn.com.title: US and China discussing reciprocal nuclear site visits amid concerns about a new arms race
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration has discussed beginning reciprocal nuclear site visits with China and plans to continue pushing for that possibility during in-person meetings in the coming months, according to sources familiar with the matter. The discussions, which have been informal and preliminary, come amid mounting US concerns about China’s rapidly growing nuclear weapons program and after the last remaining arms control agreement between the US and Russia expired last year. The effort to establish a trilateral agreement began in Trump’s first term, but no tangible progress has been made and formal talks on a new accord have not begun, with China and Russia largely ignoring substantive US outreach efforts. The idea of reciprocal visits was initially raised by the Chinese while meeting US officials this year, one source said, giving some indication that the communist nation may be open to pursuing confidence building measures that could pave the way for a grander agreement. Visits to the US Department of Energy national labs and to China’s equivalent facilities were discussed, and the US would be open to discussing visits to nuclear testing sites, the source said. The nuclear discussions between the US and Chinese officials at the working level so far this year have largely occurred on the sidelines of gatherings by the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, known as the P5, sources said. The concept of allowing nuclear site visits could move the needle on the US efforts to engage China on issues related to strategic stability and potentially serve as a building block for a trilateral agreement, but China remains adamant that they will not engage on discussions that could limit their nuclear buildup. The US currently has a much bigger nuclear arsenal with about 5,000 total nuclear warheads while China has about 600, but it is expanding its nuclear weapons infrastructure and has been projected to produce hundreds more warheads over the next decade. A State Department spokesperson referred questions to the White House, which did not provide a comment. CNN has requested comment from the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC. Last Thursday, China began its weeklong National Day holiday, during which all government offices are closed. Paul Dean, who previously served as an acting assistant secretary of state overseeing US arms control efforts, told CNN that the administration needs to approach any Chinese nuclear negotiations with its “eyes wide open,” but said that reciprocal visits would be “an extremely valuable confidence-building measure” that could lay the informational and diplomatic foundation for additional work to reduce nuclear risk between the two countries. “This is a very dangerous time, and there are very few guardrails in place on the US-China nuclear relationship,” Dean, now a vice president at the Nuclear Threat Initiative nonprofit, said. President Donald Trump expressed support for trilateral arms control negotiations between the US, Russia and China when he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, but they didn’t discuss the possibility of site visits during their talks, a US official said. Xi did not leave the door open to discussing a trilateral agreement, pointing to the US and Russian nuclear arsenals being larger than China’s – a point that Chinese officials have routinely used to shield themselves from any discussions that could lead to limiting their nuclear stockpile before they are on par with the US, the official added. Still, the topic of nuclear arms control has long been a focus for Trump, who is expected to meet with Xi twice later this year. By the time the two leaders meet again it is expected that further lower-level discussions on possible nuclear site visits will have taken place, the sources said. Visiting nuclear sites for on-site inspections have historically been used as a vital verification tool by the International Atomic Energy Agency to be sure that nations are abiding by their commitments to using the facilities for peaceful purposes. Skepticism about China’s motives Experts and former US officials who spoke with CNN were encouraged by the talks but were not confident that they will immediately lead to concrete progress on a breakthrough agreement. “It has to be taken seriously. It could be a great start,” said a former US official who has engaged China in track two discussions related to strategic stability in recent years. Still, skeptics noted that the Chinese may have floated the idea in an effort to create a positive atmosphere or to appear serious on the topic of nuclear arsenals, said former US officials and experts who questioned the authenticity of such an offer. “In advance of a big summit if the Chinese can put good feelers out there they will do that,” said another former US official who focused on nuclear issues. “It makes them seem more magnanimous as the two sides are engaging.” The Chinese may have a “maligned motivation” they said. About a year ago Trump said that the US would resume nuclear testing on an “equal basis” with China and Russia, but there has been no known US nuclear testing since that pronouncement. The administration earlier this year accused China of carrying out a secret nuclear test in 2020 using a technique known as “decoupling” designed to evade detection by firing the explosion in an empty cavern to minimize seismic shaking. The National Nuclear Security Administration’s nonproliferation directorate conducted a 16-ton underground non-nuclear explosion last week at the Nevada National Security Site that was the second in a years-long series of experiments designed to mimic the alleged Chinese test, according to an agency spokesperson. The decoupled test explosion offered NNSA and other entities a chance to validate the effectiveness of new methods and equipment for detecting such stealthy tests. “You cannot evade American innovation,” NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams said in a news release announcing the test. The Trump administration is also working on a proposal that would enable assure verification that low-yield nuclear testing is not happening at nuclear sites and could share that with the P5 group later this year, a US official said. It is unclear what kind of technical equipment could be part of that proposal. Gerald Brown, who studies China’s military at the Council on Foreign Relations nonprofit, said he is “not particularly optimistic” but that the reciprocal visit scheme, if enacted, is “a potential glimmer of hope” for reducing nuclear risk between the US and China. Brown, a former State Department intel analyst, said that China’s ongoing nuclear buildup “is deeply linked with political goals, namely its aggressive ambitions regarding Taiwan.” China historically has viewed nuclear talks as “tool to gain political concessions” on Taiwan, he argued, rather than as a genuine policy goal. “You won’t know what’s on the table until you engage in a thoughtful, rigorous way to see if this is something in our interest — and it might be,” said Dean. Dean, whose nonprofit has engaged with Chinese entities in nonofficial diplomatic discussions in recent months, said he sees mutual “interest and acknowledgement that the risks are real.” He pointed at the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, which sparked some of the first US-Soviet risk reduction measures like a 24-hour phone hotline, as a historical warning. “We don’t need to wait for a crisis to start reducing nuclear risks,” Dean argued. “And the risks are very real right now.” Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

cnn.com.title: Former German spy chief arrested on treason and espionage allegations
cnn.com.text: BERLIN (AP) — Germany’s federal prosecutor’s office said a former foreign intelligence chief was arrested Tuesday on espionage allegations. August Hanning, 80, served as president of the Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, from December 1998 to November 2005. He is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage,” the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement. Hanning was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide of his, identified only as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany. He is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage. The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for. The prosecutor’s office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning’s chief of staff. After Hanning’s tenure at the BND, he went on to serve as chief of staff for several subsequent presidents of the BND from March 2012 until March 2026. “In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor’s office said. Both suspects are believed to have agreed, in the spring of 2010, to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning “in exchange for remuneration.” “The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement alleges. Hanning used the information in his private consulting work, the statement added. The office said “on one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service.” The office did not say which country the foreign agent worked for and added that “it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient.” The premises of both men were searched Tuesday.

cnn.com.title: Nobel Prize in physics awarded to Francis Halzen for his work detecting ‘ghostly’ cosmic particles
cnn.com.text: The 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has been awarded to Francis Halzen, a pioneering Belgian astrophysicist whose work developing a massive observatory in Antarctica to detect “ghostly” cosmic particles  laid the foundations for an “entirely new type of astronomy.” These tiny, high-energy particles from space, known as neutrinos, transmit information which allow scientists to better understand distant galaxies and exploding stars, said Nobel committee member Eva Olsson at the award presentation on Tuesday at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. “Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument,” said Nobel committee chair Mark Pearce in a statement. “His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.” Halzen, 82, told the Nobel news conference by phone from Italy that it was a “great surprise” and “pleasure” to win the award. “When we started this project, everybody realized this was maybe a good idea but very few thought it would work, including myself,” he said. “So this was kind of an adventure where success wasn’t guaranteed.” The professor, who is based at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, first presented plans for the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in 1988, envisioning a vast network of sensors in Antarctic ice that could capture neutrinos. The observatory harnesses a key property of neutrinos — that they produce a flash of light when colliding with an atomic nucleus which could be tracked by sensors embedded in clear, glacial ice. Arriving at Earth from the far reaches of the cosmos, neutrinos are often called “ghostly” because they are extremely volatile, or vaporous, and can go through any kind of matter without changing. They have almost no mass, and no electrical charge. They can travel through the most extreme environments, like stars, planets and entire galaxies, and remain the same. “It’s been a while since the Nobel Prize has gone to a single individual and that points to the uniqueness of his vision,” said Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, which is published by the American Institute of Physics. “It took a team of hundreds of people to build it, but it all started with one person.” Observatory in the ice While billions of neutrinos originate from the sun, neutrinos that come from other regions of space are much rarer and harder to detect. In the 1980s, Halzen first realized that Antarctic ice could be ideal for trapping these secretive neutrinos but installing sensitive equipment deep in the ice was a huge endeavor requiring researchers to drill kilometer-deep holes and lower strings of light sensors. IceCube’s predecessor, known as AMANDA, was completed in 2000 but it didn’t manage to detect the high-energy neutrinos Halzen was looking for, the Nobel Committee said. Work then began on IceCube – a cubic kilometre of ice equipped with light sensors, which reached its full size in 2011, with 5,160 light sensors divided between 86 cables. In 2013, the research team reported the first evidence to support the detection of cosmic neutrinos and a couple of years later, they had gathered enough data to be certain of their discovery. The Nobel committee said IceCube would take neutrino astronomy to a new level, providing information about cosmic phenomena that are hidden behind dust clouds and distant space objects such as black holes. A project to expand IceCube, allowing it to monitor eight cubic kilometers of ice, is planned. Last year, the physics prize went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for their discovery of a phenomenon called quantum mechanical tunneling in an electrical circuit, an advance that laid the foundation for quantum computing and other related technology. The prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million). On Monday, the Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded to three scientists for their work developing a technique to decode the inner workings of the brain. The awards continue on Wednesday with the announcement of the chemistry prize, followed by literature on Thursday. The peace prize will be revealed on Friday, followed by the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on October 12. This story and its headline has been updated with additional reporting.

cnn.com.title: Wall Street is booming. Surging yields could shake things up
cnn.com.text: Wall Street rolled into 2026 on a hot streak and continued with a booming first half. Profits surged, fueled by massive spending on artificial intelligence, elevated trading activity in a volatile market and dealmaking that has benefited from a relaxed regulatory environment under the Trump administration. Wall Street hauled in $45.9 billion in profits in the first half of the year, up 51% from the same period a year ago, according to the New York State Comptroller’s latest report on the securities industry in New York City. At the current pace of growth, the industry’s profits in 2026 could exceed $90 billion for the full year — smashing through previous records and outpacing the inflation-adjusted record set in 2009. The boon for traders and bankers comes as AI investment is fueling US economic growth even as consumer sentiment hovers at historic lows due to concerns about the cost of living, from rising energy prices to stubborn food inflation. “Despite geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty, the industry has remained resilient,” Thomas P. DiNapoli, New York State Comptroller and author of the report, said in a statement. The good times are expected to keep rolling, but risks remain. The financial industry has a lingering obstacle to deal with: rising interest rates. The key 10-year Treasury yield, which sets interest rates across the economy, hit 5.35% on Monday — its highest level since 2002. The recent rise in interest rates “may dampen profitability” if dealmaking slows down or firms’ interest liabilities rise significantly, DiNapoli noted. The surge in bond yields is pushing up the cost of borrowing from mortgages to auto loans, which can weigh on economic activity. Higher yields can also raise risks for the stock market and put a chill on the hot IPO and dealmaking market. “Rising yields for bonds issued by the U.S. and other governments in recent weeks are another concerning indicator for investors,” DiNapoli wrote in the report. Wall Street rides the AI wave The New York City comptroller’s office had forecasted in May that Wall Street would earn $45.3 billion in profits for the entire year — a figure that has already been surpassed. The surge in profits has been driven by robust trading in stocks, bonds and currencies, fees from supervising and advising clients’ investments, underwriting initial public offerings and a pickup in mergers and acquisitions. “Investment in AI companies continues to drive the market,” DiNapoli wrote. AI-related venture capital spending hit $407 billion in the first half of the year, more than 50% higher than the annual total of $264 billion in 2025, the report found. The AI boom, a pickup in M&A and a series of IPOs have created a sweet backdrop for earnings. Revenues from underwriting activities — like IPOs — rose 68% year-over-year in the first half of 2026, the report found. Anthropic, a powerhouse AI company that could be valued at $2 trillion, is expected to go public this year, creating another major opportunity for Wall Street banks to haul in fees from underwriting and trading activity. Wall Street’s fortunes have also been aided by a business-friendly administration in the White House, DiNapoli said. The boosts to companies’ bottom lines are reflected in growing salaries: The average annual salary (including bonuses) in New York City’s securities industry rose 11.1% to $561,770 in 2025. The bonus pool last year reached $49.2 billion, the report found, equivalent to an average bonus of $246,900 per employee, up 6% from the previous year. Wall Street’s windfall is also a boon for New York State and City tax revenues. The industry’s contribution to New York City tax collections rose 15.8% in the 2026 fiscal year compared to the prior year. “Commensurate with record industry profitability, tax collections related to securities continue to reach new levels,” DiNapoli wrote in the report. Still, bond market volatility has picked up in recent weeks. The rise in interest rates could put pressure on Wall Street firms’ trading returns, while also dampening the outlook for the IPO market and dealmaking, as well as the consumer. Wall Street is at the center of the AI boom, but is also exposed to any downturn or fading enthusiasm. “While the industry continues to see strong profits, there are growing concerns regarding ongoing geopolitical conflicts, inflation and interest rates, the outsized contributions of the burgeoning AI sector and the deregulatory push of the current administration,” DiNapoli wrote. He added that “the potential for an industry downturn presents an increasing risk to public finances and the broader regional economy.”

cnn.com.title: ‘Let Troy be Troy’: How Maine Democrats’ hope to beat Sen. Susan Collins is working to quiet doubters
cnn.com.text: As Democrats enter the homestretch of their longtime quest to defeat Maine GOP Sen. Susan Collins, they are placing their hope in a fifth-generation logger from the state’s rural north who speaks with a distinct Allagash accent, displays an apparent penchant for boba tea and has never been this close to the national spotlight before. This was not how it was supposed to go. But more than two months after Democrats picked Troy Jackson to replace Graham Platner following allegations of sexual assault that Platner has denied, his supporters, critics and other observers agree on one thing. “Troy is definitely unusual,” said Douglas Rooks, a longtime Maine writer and historian who worked in the state legislature when Jackson first arrived there in 2002. “He is very different from anybody who’s been elected in a long, long time from Maine and many other places.” Jackson’s quirkiness is set to be tested in a crucial period of the campaign beginning Tuesday night, when he and Collins are set to meet for the first of four debates in 10 days. And this weekend, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) is set to visit Maine for three rallies with Jackson, testing whether the progressive working-class politics they share play as well in a general election as they do in a primary. “[Jackson] is who he is, and I think in this election, people like that,” said Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington. But he also said Jackson would have a “learning curve” on navigating the Senate compared to Collins that could work against him. Jackson has hit a few road bumps recently. A September story from New York magazine aired out concerns he’s being overly managed by out-of-state consultants, a video of him enjoying a boba tea drew widespread ridicule online, and he had to apologize for theorizing about why Jews may not want to call the war in Gaza a genocide. A CBS News/YouGov poll released Friday showed some warning signs for Jackson. Forty-three percent of Democrats said they wished someone else were their nominee, and nearly a fifth of voters who disapproved of Trump said they still supported Collins. The poll found the Senate race tied. Jackson, who lost his primary bid for Maine governor earlier this year before the Senate nomination came open, is still working to galvanize some former Platner loyalists. Scott Niemi, an organizer who met with Platner in August to pitch him on a write-in campaign that Platner ultimately rejected, said he supports Jackson but raised questions about his ability to excite Democrats. “Obviously he doesn’t carry the same energy as Graham, and he definitely doesn’t have the speaking ability that Graham did,” Niemi said. “I think that’s kind of hurt him the most. We went from someone who’s fiery, had a lot of fight in him, to a guy who’s a bit on the calm side, which I can appreciate, but we want someone who can go to Washington and fight for us.” Jackson has insisted he is staying the course. “Nothing has changed,” Jackson said during a call-in program on Maine radio Thursday when asked about the New York magazine story. “This campaign has the same people working on it that it did during the governor’s race. At the end of the day, this campaign is for anyone and everyone who wants to beat Susan Collins and Donald Trump and have a government that works for them.” Cathy Breen, a Jackson supporter who served with him in the state Senate, said he is “in brand new waters, which I’m sure is disorienting.” But she said she was confident in his campaign and strategy, noting he “absolutely knows what happened” in 2020 when Maine Democrats nominated a more traditional politician, state House Speaker Sara Gideon, and had their hopes dashed by Collins. “Mainers can smell Washington like nobody’s business, and they don’t like Washington telling them what they do,” Breen said. “I think Troy’s done a really good job of staying true to his story.” Jackson has made at least 50 public appearances since he replaced Platner in late July, according to his campaign. He has leaned into making the race a referendum on Collins’ support for Supreme Court justices who helped overturn Roe v. Wade, an issue that national Democrats believe is key to peeling off women who have historically broken for Collins. Democrats were at least initially excited that Jackson mixed Platner’s outside image with far more government and political experience. But Republicans are working to use his resume against him. “The fact is, Troy is a 20-year Augusta insider, which poses a problem for him, since Mainers know that’s where so many of their biggest problems come from,” Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said in a statement. Collins remains under pressure to answer for a recent ProPublica story detailing an alleged pay-to-play scheme involving her office, a report she’s strenuously disputed. And President Donald Trump continues to be a major vulnerability for her in a state where he is deeply unpopular. Some Jackson supporters say his mission is to strike more of a balance between his Aroostook County folksiness and the gravitas that Mainers have come to expect from their senators, including on policy issues. Rooks said the transition from the small world of state politics – the Maine Legislature is part-time – to a federal race can trip up politicians and cause “a lot of vertigo.” “If I were helping him with debate prep, which I am not, my thing would be, ‘let Troy be Troy,’ and let’s just make sure on substance, he’s sharp,” said Nirav Shah, who also tried to replace Platner but dropped out as Maine Democrats coalesced around Jackson.

cnn.com.title: Three wild dogs traveled more than 2,500 miles just to find a mate
cnn.com.text: Worn down by the endless swiping on apps, it’s easy to understand why many on the hunt for love are deeply disillusioned by the state of modern dating. Yet one real-life epic love story has proven that romance is still very much alive, kicking and ­— in this case — tail wagging. Driven by the desire for a partner, three male African wild dogs left the safety of their pack in Zambia to embark upon a 2,563-mile odyssey fraught with danger, to find mates. Crossing crocodile-infested rivers while evading the threat of lions and humans alike, the young brothers covered a distance roughly 249 miles shy of the width of the United States in under nine months. When the trek finally culminated in April, the wild dogs set a record for the longest documented single land journey by any animal on the continent, rewriting our understanding of the connectivity between faraway populations of an intensely social species. Some 9,300 miles away at Montana State University, Scott Creel, a professor of conservation biology and ecology, followed the trio’s journey — beamed via GPS tracking collars — on his laptop. “You check every day, and you’re like, ‘Yeah, this is extraordinary,’” Creel, who co-authored a study on their journey, published last month in The Scientific Naturalist, told CNN. With fewer than 700 packs and under 1,700 mature individuals left globally, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), African wild dogs are classified as endangered and are proving increasingly difficult for researchers to find. Their behavior complicates the challenge; home ranges span hundreds of square miles, spacing packs out across the continent, and breeding is typically limited to a single dominant individual from each sex within each pack. Eventually, the rest of the pack must make a choice: stick around and wait for the chance to become the alpha male or female, potentially when one of the head pair dies, or break from the group in search of a mate to start a new family in a process known as dispersal. On August 6, 2025, the trio of three-year-old males, born and raised among the Mayukuyuku pack in western Zambia’s Kafue National Park, chose option two. “If there’s no opportunities amongst the packs that are their immediate neighbors, they just sort of pick a direction and go,” explained Creel. “Then they’re just rolling with the punches.” Travel mode The brothers were three of more than 500 African wild dogs from over 50 packs that Creel, in collaboration with the Zambian Carnivore Programme, spent the past 16 years studying via satellite GPS radio collars that track the animals’ movements across their entire life. Their departure did not come as a shock. Three of 19 pups to survive to adulthood, the males’ chances of breeding were low in a large pack and four of their agemate sisters had dispersed two weeks prior. Yet the nature and scale of the subsequent journey was unprecedented. Within a month, the males had ventured hundreds of miles toward the country’s urban center, swiftly doubling back on each occasion they reached the outskirts of major cities like Kabwe. When leaving the national parks and other protected areas to enter regions with a higher human footprint, the dogs’ movement patterns revealed a dramatic shift that Creel hypothesizes as “travel mode.” A moderate balance of moving, resting, hunting was replaced by an accelerated linear approach adopted to speed around potential danger, a behavior which Creel believes evolved from responses to run-ins with lions. The males reunited with their sisters — by then down to three — midway through September, almost 750 miles from their starting point in the northerly Copperbelt Province, a testament to the dogs’ ability to locate each other via scent. After a day with their siblings, the trio spent the next six months on a winding route westward before reaching a forested region in eastern Zambia Luangwa Valley, home to one of the largest African wild dog populations on the continent, where they remained. Creel believes it is likely the dogs connected with females, though the difficulty of accessing the highly remote area means research teams have been unable to conclusively verify the union. Yet the long-range treks made by the Mayukuyuku siblings and other tracked wild dogs is ample cause for conservationists to be excited. Movements of dispersed, collared individuals have connected all of Zambia’s resident wild dog populations, spanning seven national parks. What’s more, there are examples of the species’ connectivity extending to the broader sub-Saharan region. The sisters crossed into Mozambique and since then, another group of Mayukuyuku dispersers crossed north into the Democratic Republic of Congo, while a group from a different pack headed east into Malawi. It is a “mind-boggling” level of linkage that Creel “would not have dreamed of” still enduring today when he began studying the dogs, and a source of optimism that their continued ability to make new connections — despite the distances and human populations in between — means there is hope for their dwindling numbers to rise naturally. “They’ll only recover if they’re connected,” said Creel. “There’ll be nothing left to save” That is Creel’s “glass half full” takeaway from the long-distance wild dog journeys. The other side of the story is written in blood. A few weeks after reuniting with the brothers, one of the three surviving Mayukuyuku females was caught in a wire snare while traversing through a forest. Anchored to trees, the noose is designed to catch an animal and then tighten, often inflicting a “horror show” of injuries in the process as the abrasive wire bites into flesh as deep as three inches, Creel explained. The snares are not intended to catch African wild dogs, but are set by bushmeat poachers in pursuit of large herbivores like wildebeest or zebra. Even when wild dogs and lions manage to bite their way free, many still succumb to their wounds. “You set it, and then whoever walks through the gap in the bushes next is who dies,” Creel said. “If you see the damage that they do, it’s very hard not to be engaged,” he added. “I can’t imagine how painful it is.” With wild dogs unable to recognize wire snares (some dogs have been snared as often as four times) and reluctant to leave behind fallen packmates, tracking data showed the two other Mayukuyuku sisters returning to their mortally wounded sibling before one of the pair stopped moving for good. A GPS collar, cut off by a knife, was later found at the site, leading researchers to conclude that she, too, had died in a snare. With the remaining sister not wearing a collar, her fate is unknown. It is an all too familiar tragedy for Creel. When he started working in Tanzania almost four decades ago, he would head out with his wife and remove as many as 500 snares in a matter of days. He believes the issue has intensified since then, and fears the ramifications if solutions aren’t found to a “complicated problem.” “If we don’t get on top of that, there’ll be nothing left to save,” he said. “People don’t snare because it’s a fun hobby. They do it because they’re poor people living at the end of a long dirt road without a lot of options. So I’m not talking just about law enforcement. I’m also talking about finding ways to make it unnecessary.” The greatest ramification of snares for wild dogs is not the direct threat to them, but to their prey. The decline of large herbivore populations across sub-Saharan Africa due to bushmeat poaching is forcing the canines to work harder and roam farther in search of food, a 2025 research paper co-authored by Creel found, in turn increasing their risk of becoming ensnared. It is sobering reality check for anyone romanticizing the wild dogs’ journey like it’s a Disney movie. Yet Creel does not dismiss people who anthropomorphize these animals; he remains deeply invested in their survival. “It’s pretty hard not to have some empathy for what a difficult task these animals face in the world as we’ve made it,” he said. “There’s 8.3 billion of us, but we’re sharing the world with almost 8 million other species. I care a lot about that.”

cnn.com.title: This city is on track to run out of water by 2030. For many residents, that day is already here
cnn.com.text: Shazia knows what life will be like in a major city that’s run out of water because she’s already living that reality — and it’s unbearable. The 34-year-old lives in the Khair Khana neighborhood of Afghanistan’s capital Kabul with her three children and her husband, who ekes out a living as a street vendor. They have no running water and can’t afford to buy it from the water tankers that often outnumber cars on the city streets. Every day she and her kids must walk to a local mosque and wait in hour-long lines to fill buckets from a hand pump, before heading back with their heavy loads. Her back aches and she hates having to drag her kids out after school, “but we have no choice,” she said. Kabul is on track to be the first modern city to run out of water, and could do so as soon as 2030, according to a recent report from the nonprofit Prosper Global. But for Shazia, and many other residents across this fast-expanding city, that day is already here. They are on the frontlines of a spiraling urban water crisis that isn’t confined to Kabul. Cities across the world — from Corpus Christi, Texas, to Iran’s capital Tehran — are teetering on the edge of water shortages so severe that residents are bracing for a “day zero,” the point at which taps run dry for large parts of the city. Their crises tend to follow familiar beats: Booming populations colliding with insufficient, underfunded water infrastructure. Beneath it all hums the climate crisis, driving hotter, drier weather and pushing the water cycle off balance. Of all the urban areas facing day zero, Kabul’s situation may be starkest. It’s one of the fastest-growing cities, located in one of the most climate-vulnerable countries. Afghanistan has also suffered from decades of conflict and global aid has all but dried up since the return of Taliban rule in 2021. Kabul is staring down a “human catastrophe,” said Mohd Faizee, a professor at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health. “We have only a limited window of time.” Those who want to understand what the future of water looks like in our changing world should look to Kabul. The search for water beneath the ground On the streets of Kabul, water is a huge topic of conversation, said Mirza Jan, who lives in the city’s Taimani neighborhood. Everyone is affected. When Jan’s family bought their house in 1990, they could pull up water by hand in a bucket from a shallow well. Over the years, he has had to dig the well down farther and farther as it kept drying up. It’s now more than 700 feet deep, an expensive endeavor only possible because of money sent by his two sons who live in the US. As groundwater shrinks, those like Jan who can afford the upfront cost keep digging deeper; those who can’t rely on expensive tanker water or hand pumps at mosques. None of these options are sustainable. “It is an invisible catastrophe in the making,” Jan said, “the city will soon run completely out of water.” Kabul should not be water scarce. Sprawled across a wide valley, it is framed by the Hindu Kush Himalaya. The rugged peaks of Afghanistan’s section of this vast mountain range act as water towers. Melting snow and glacial ice feed the Kabul River, which cuts through the city, and recharge aquifers, which form the backbone of the city’s water system, supplying 80% of residents. Just a fifth have access to piped water. Over the past decade, however, groundwater levels have plummeted nearly 100 feet, according to Prosper Global. Water is now being pumped out far faster than it can be replenished, leaving an estimated shortfall of more than 1.55 billion cubic feet a year. Nearly half the city’s boreholes have dried up. “In many neighbourhoods, water has already run out,” Faizee said It’s the result of soaring demand, from homes, greenhouses and businesses. But the human-caused climate crisis also plays a role. The country has endured six consecutive years of drought, with last year one of its most severe. Snowfall reached a 25-year low in Afghanistan at the end of last year, according to UN data, and it’s part of a long-term trend which has seen snow levels fall by nearly 20% between 2014 and 2020. When the rain does fall, Kabul’s hard, impermeable surfaces mean the water doesn’t replenish aquifers, but instead sweeps through the city as flash floods, destroying homes, killing people and rolling away. Kabul’s vanishing groundwater isn’t a crisis, said Najibullah Sadid, a Germany-based water and environment researcher with the Afghanistan Water and Environment Professionals Network. That word implies a short-term shock to the system. He prefers the term “water bankruptcy” because “you’re running out of a resource which is not recoverable anymore.” Unchecked expansion Said Agha and his family live in an apartment in the densely packed Kabul neighborhood of Karte Naw. He makes decent money working for a company, but the city’s water crisis spares few. His building is home to 14 families but relies on one well that dries up every few months. Most of the time they only have running water for short bursts. Sometimes it’s off for days. Agha is convinced the city’s aquifers will soon run dry and he doesn’t know what to do. His job is tied to Kabul and leaving would be a “calamity,” he said. Kabul is expanding vertically, with multistory buildings stacked on top of existing structures. Instead of one family on a plot of land, there are now dozens and it’s dramatically increasing pressure on already strained water resources, Sadid said. Kabul is one of the fastest growing cities in the world. Experts estimate its population has ballooned from less than 1 million in 2001 to 6 million today. People have gravitated there for different reasons. Many returned after the fall of the Taliban in 2001, in the hopes of better opportunities. More recently, there’s been a surge due to the large-scale expulsion of Afghans from neighboring Iran and Pakistan amid increasing regional tensions. People are also migrating to the city from rural regions, in search of jobs and sometimes, ironically, a better water situation. As water runs out, residents pay For the last two years, Asadullah Ahmadi has been spending at least 150 Afghanis ($2.35) a day, a big chunk of his income, to get enough water for his family of seven. Even then, the water they get is dirty and must be boiled. “It is not sustainable, and I don’t know how long we can afford this,” he said. Running out of water is expensive. Many in Kabul, like Ahmadi, are forced to rely on tanked in water from private companies. Some of these companies are motivated to help people, but others are simply looking for big profits, said Marianna von Zahn, the former Afghanistan director of programs at Prosper Global. They pump groundwater and sell it back to residents at inflated prices. The impacts are most acute for residents already facing high levels of poverty, said a UN official based in Afghanistan. That’s “the most dangerous part” of the situation, they said. Poorer people are spending up to 30% of their total income on water, analysts estimate. The UN considers affordable water costs to be 3% or less of household income. To add to the dire situation, up to 80% of large parts of the city’s groundwater is contaminated, both by sewage and by naturally occurring substances such as arsenic. It’s “another hidden crisis.” said Jalal Naser Faqiryar, a Netherlands-based water specialist and former director general of Kabul River Basin. Kabul residents have few options. Ahmadi fears he’ll need to abandon his home but “even if I do leave, where can I go in search of water? The whole city is suffering from this problem.” Some may leave Kabul altogether, but water scarcity is common in many parts of Afghanistan. And leaving the country is fraught with difficulty. Neighboring Iran and Pakistan are forcibly returning Afghans, and further afield in Europe, fervent anti-immigration rhetoric makes the situation very challenging. “There’s not really anywhere to go,” the UN official said. Attempts to harness rivers and rain There are plans to help alleviate Kabul’s impending catastrophe by harnessing surface water. The Shahtoot Dam, which would be built on a tributary of the Kabul River, could provide water for more than 2 million people in the city. India agreed to fund it, but the project stalled after the Taliban’s return to power in 2021. The Taliban insists it’s going ahead imminently but construction has yet to begin, and it faces steep opposition from Pakistan, which claims the dam will significantly reduce the water it receives from the Kabul River. Another plan is a 124-mile pipeline that would transport water from the Panjshir River to Kabul, to supply 2 million city residents. But it’s still at the survey and design stage. Even if these projects move ahead, they would take years to construct and would also require treatment plants and a proper network to bring the water into people’s homes. “The Taliban do not have the capacity to deal with a problem this big, and they know it,” Faizee said. Kabul’s water situation is “heading toward a serious crisis,” said Matiullah Abid, the spokesman for the Afghanistan Ministry of Energy and Water. He said the ministry is acting, including by constructing dams and thousands of wells in the city to recharge groundwater, controlling commercial water use and completing the Shah wa Arous Dam in 2024, designed to supply 20,000 households. There are many ongoing efforts to tackle the water problem but “these measures require time and resources,” Abid added. People ‘continue to suffer silently’ The Taliban, itself, is an added complication in Kabul’s water story. It is not recognized as a legitimate government by most of the international community due to its human rights abuses, including stripping away the rights of women and girls. As a result, international aid has plummeted, even as Kabul and other parts Afghanistan edge toward water disaster. The world is “watching the crisis unfold” instead of preventing it now, Faizee said. “Later, it will pay for the emergency response, such as water trucking, disease outbreaks and displacement.” For now, people will “continue to suffer silently,” said Susanne Schmeier, professor of water cooperation, law, and diplomacy at IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands. Kabul shows what a day zero looks like. It’s not every single tap suddenly running dry, it’s a slow-moving catastrophe that sees residents forced into ever-harder decisions. Do they sink money into expensive, deeper wells that will inevitably run dry, or rely on private water tankers that push them further into poverty? Do they make arduous, daily journeys to hand pumps, taking kids away from schoolwork and play, while also risking their physical health and safety? Or, do they move away from the city and their jobs, and risk finding themselves in an equally bad water situation? What’s happening offers a snapshot of what may be coming for many other cities, as climate change meets urban water systems built for a very different world. For Kabul residents, it’s trauma on top of trauma. “Years ago, we were running away from bombs and rockets in Kabul,” said city resident Said Agha. “Now we may have to flee because of a lack of water.”

cnn.com.title: Democrats are taking big chunks of GOP voters in key Senate races, polls show
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump has never had worse poll numbers with his base than he does ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. And a growing volume of polls shows a significant portion of that base is preparing to cross over and vote for Democrats. New York Times-Siena College polls released over the weekend showed between 9% and 16% of Republican likely voters said they favored the Democratic nominee in five key states: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas. And these aren’t the only polls to show a sizable crossover effect — especially in the middle of the country. All told, Democratic candidates have led among GOP voters by double digits in four key Senate races, and they lead by an average of at least 9 points in seven of the top 10 races, according to a CNN review of polling in each state. Democratic candidates also seem poised to take an especially large percentage of Republican voters who don’t identify with Trump’s MAGA movement — often around one-quarter of them. This data comes with an important caveat: Polling in the last few presidential elections has underestimated GOP support. And there are some signs that those misses may have been driven by polls reaching the right number of Republicans overall, but not enough of the party’s — and by extension, Trump’s — strongest supporters. If that pattern holds this year, it’s possible that GOP-aligned voters may wind up more supportive of Republican candidates than the polls suggest now. But it is worth noting that polling in the last midterm election, in 2022, did not exhibit this pattern. Perhaps the most striking numbers in the new Times-Siena polls came in Kansas, which has recently emerged as a surprising battleground. The poll showed Democrat Adam Hamilton tied with GOP Sen. Roger Marshall at 45% among likely voters, with the Libertarian candidate at 5%. So how has Hamilton made the race that close in red Kansas, a state that Trump carried by 16 points in 2024? The pastor has peeled off 16% of registered Republicans and 10% of self-identified Republicans. (By contrast, Marshall took just 2-3% of each category of Democrats, according to the survey.) But Hamilton is not the only Democratic candidate pulling double digits among Republican voters. The Times-Siena poll showed Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek taking 12% of registered Republicans and 5% of self-identified Republicans. And the state representative also took double digits among self-identified Republicans in recent polls from Marist College (13%) and Fox News (10%). In Alaska, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola took 13% of registered Republicans and 9% of self-identified Republicans in the Times-Siena poll. And in Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff was taking 10% of self-identified Republicans in the most recent high-quality poll, from Fox News in late June. Other Democrats take slightly less but still significant numbers. The Democratic nominees in North Carolina (Roy Cooper), Ohio (Sherrod Brown) and Texas (James Talarico) have all averaged 9% of the GOP vote in recent high-quality polls, according to a CNN review. Among other Democrats: New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas was averaging 5%, former Maine state Senate President Troy Jackson was averaging 4%, and Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed was averaging 3%. Thus far, the Democratic Party hasn’t matched the larger advantages in national polling. The so-called generic ballot, which asks people to choose between an unnamed Republican and an unnamed Democrat, shows Democrats averaging about 4% of Republican voters in recent high-quality polls. But the numbers do recall some of Democrats’ results in the 2018 midterms, which was a strong year for Democrats overall. Exit polls back then showed Democrats taking double digits’ worth of GOP voters in a number of states — West Virginia (17%), Arizona (12%), Ohio (11%), Pennsylvania (11%) and Wisconsin (10%) — and taking between 5% and 9% in the rest of the key races. (While Democrats took more than 40 House seats from the GOP and benefitted from a favorable environment in the first midterm election under Trump, they did lose two Senate seats because they were defending some very red states.) This year, Fox News polling also breaks out Republicans between MAGA Republicans and non-MAGA Republicans. And four Democratic Senate candidates have taken at least 21% of the non-MAGA Republicans: Cooper in North Carolina (21%), Talarico in Texas (22%), Brown in Ohio (25%) and Turek in Iowa (28%). El-Sayed took 12% of non-MAGA Republicans in Michigan, while Democrats took 12% on the most recent national generic ballot. And given Trump’s apparent base problems, if Democrats do have a historic night on November 3, that could be a group of voters we’ll be talking a lot about in the aftermath.

cnn.com.title: Quebec separatists vowing independence vote win provincial election but fall short of majority
cnn.com.text: The separatist Parti Québécois won Quebec’s provincial election Monday but fell short of enough seats to govern alone, returning to power with a promise to hold another referendum on independence from Canada. The result returns Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party to power for the first time in more than a decade but denies it the majority it sought, forcing the separatists to rely on opposition parties even as they try to revive Quebec’s independence debate. The party was on track to win nearly 60 seats as the final votes were counted, falling short of the 64 needed for a majority in Quebec’s 127-member National Assembly, the provincial legislature. A minority government means PQ will need support from opposition lawmakers to pass key legislation and survive confidence votes. St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged that voters had denied his party a majority. “Quebecers elected the Parti Québécois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message,” he said. Leader wants an independence vote He has pledged to hold another referendum on independence, though he has said he would wait until US President Donald Trump is no longer in office. St-Pierre Plamondon framed independence as essential to preserving Quebec’s French-speaking identity, saying it was a “question of survival” for a French-speaking population that represents only a small fraction of North America. He said Quebec “just wants to exist on its own like other countries of the world” and that a referendum would allow Quebecers to decide their own future. “I continue to dream and visualize that country,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. “That dream will be realized one day.” He also sought to reassure Canadians outside Quebec. “The project for independence is not about excluding you,” he said. “Quebec will never change its geographical position, so we have an interest in working together.” Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette conceded defeat, saying voters had made their choice and that she took full responsibility for the “difficult result.” The CAQ, which entered the election with 79 seats, was shut out of the legislature, and Fréchette lost her own seat in Trois-Rivières. Victory is not a mandate for independence But the PQ’s victory does not mean most Quebecers support leaving Canada. “This was not an election about independence, which is not popular in Quebec right now, but about getting rid of the CAQ, the party in power since 2018,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. Support for independence remains at about 30%, low by historical standards, he said. Béland said the minority result is likely welcome news for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government because it could make it harder for the PQ to prepare for and eventually call an independence referendum. The PQ would face opposition from both the Liberals and Conservatives, whose leaders have said they would fight efforts to hold a sovereignty referendum. Québec solidaire, another pro-independence party, could hold the balance of power and potentially support the PQ on a referendum. Carney congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and signaled that Ottawa would work with the incoming separatist government. “Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada,” Carney said. He said the two governments would work together to support businesses and workers affected by US tariffs, create jobs and build housing. Quebec result adds to Canada’s national-unity questions Still, Béland said a separatist government in Quebec poses a new national-unity challenge for Carney, particularly with another independence-related vote approaching elsewhere in Canada. The Quebec result comes two weeks before Albertans vote October 19 on whether to hold a referendum on separation from Canada. “Seeing that a pro-independence party won in Quebec barely two weeks before an independence-related referendum takes place in Alberta might suggest to the Trump administration that national unity remains a major issue in Canada despite the popularity of Mark Carney,” Béland said. Quebec voters have twice rejected sovereignty, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum. Quebec, which is about 80% French-speaking, already has significant autonomy. The province of 9.1 million collects its own income tax, has immigration policies favoring French speakers and has laws giving the French language priority over English. Even with the PQ victory, Trump’s tariffs and 51st-state rhetoric have complicated the separatist argument by stirring Canadian nationalism and giving some French-speaking Quebecers another reason to value remaining part of Canada. Trump’s tariffs and repeated threats against Canada became a defining issue in the 2025 federal election, helping lift Carney’s Liberals to victory after the party had trailed badly before Trump returned to office.

cnn.com.title: Unprecedented student protests are rocking France. Here’s why they’re angry
cnn.com.text: France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis. Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 5,000 people have been taken into police custody, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye. The next big test for the government will come Tuesday when thousands of people are expected to join protest marches across the country. Here’s what to know What’s going on? The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire. “It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.” Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement. Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law. The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced. A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class. What is the government’s response? Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melanchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million). There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.” The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward. The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook. The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment. Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.” The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.

cnn.com.title: Trump backed Iran into a corner. The regime isn’t blinking
