"Pneumonic plague can transmit from person to person and that is why there is the concern around this," he said.
He added: "But of course people's thought with any outbreak of infectious disease at all runs to... lockdowns and Covid and that is just not what's going to happen here."
"People think, 'Oh the plague, that's gone, that went hundreds of years ago,' but it hasn't," Clarke said.
"It's still around and in certain parts of the world, it's a threat to human health and that's why they need to study it."
Asked if the pathogen might have been studied for potential use as a bio-weapon, the scientist agreed it was possible.
"Because this is Russia people's thoughts are running to that, but I think my earlier explanation is probably more likely," Clarke said.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
- infected flea bites
- contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
- the inhalation of respiratory particles.
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.

bbc.com.title: Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Yemeni military also said in a statement that its forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes.
But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources later told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces had only reached the city's outskirts.
The Houthis denied losing Bab al-Mandab and Mokha and said they had struck Riyadh's airport and other locations in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the air strikes.
Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks and reiterated calls for the UN Security Council's permanent members to support Yemen's internationally-recognised government.
Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, meanwhile held an emergency meeting in Riyadh and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces to Saudi Arabia in an invocation of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, according to a statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP.
The offensive launched by the pro-government National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces in south-western Yemen on Monday reportedly saw the Houthis pushed out of most of the coastal areas they seized last month.
Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating.
Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said: "Our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area."
Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town.
Houthi‑run media cited a Houthi military source as rejecting as "Saudi propaganda" the claims that the group had lost control of Mokha, and that the group remained in control of Dhubab, Bab al‑Mandab and the Kahboub mountains near the coast.
The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital, Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive.
Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.
Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences".
The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations".
On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.
The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.
In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram.
According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.
A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.
Additional reporting by Ottilie Mitchell

bbc.com.title: Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Every morning at 6am, 10-year-old Rafeef and her younger brother get ready for school, putting on their cream and brown uniforms.
She always looks forward to seeing her friends and learning about everything from maths to Arabic and Islamic studies. She can't wait to start studying English next year.
But for Rafeef, the journey to school involves far greater risks than crossing roads or missing the bus.
Her school in Taiz, south-western Yemen, stands on a mountain at the edge of a valley known as no-man's land - a heavily contested front line in the civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis.
On one side of the school is government-held territory, on the other are Houthi sniper positions.
Rafeef's home is further down the mountain.
Every time she goes to school, she has to walk uphill with her back towards the snipers. "I'm afraid," she says.
According to Unicef, roughly 3.2 million children in Yemen were out of school even before the war escalated last month.
It says thousands of children have been killed or maimed since the war began in 2014, while thousands more have been recruited by armed groups on both sides.
Yet despite the risks, Rafeef says she does not want to stop going because she loves seeing her friends and it is her only chance to be with them. She begins naming the children in her classroom.
Going to school is the only time Rafeef's parents let her go outside. They say they are keen for her to get an education and have the chance of a better life. Rafeef hopes to become a doctor.
'A mortar came out of nowhere'
Rafeef's family moved to Taiz from the coastal city of Hudaydah nine years ago, seeking safety when Houthis took control there.
But Taiz has also endured fighting.
Rafeef says that two years ago there was a mortar attack outside her new home.
"Everyone was out except for me and my brother. Then a mortar came out of nowhere… shrapnel blew through the door and into the house." Her arm was broken and there is still a scar where she was hit.
And in recent days the conflict has intensified. On Sunday the Houthis cut off a vital supply route linking Taiz to Aden, which meant they were able to effectively encircle Taiz. Control of that route has kept shifting.
Residents have told the BBC they are afraid the Houthis could seize the city at any moment.
Government forces have made gains in other areas this week, they say, retaking control of strategic points on the Bab al-Mandab Strait - a key shipping chokepoint - and launching an offensive to try to regain control of the capital, Sanaa.
Homes in Taiz are mostly scattered across the slopes, but many have been abandoned by families fleeing the fighting.
Twice, we try to visit the neighbourhood where Rafeef and her family live, but a community leader advises us it is too dangerous.
On the first occasion, residents of the neighbourhood tell us that three people have been shot by snipers. On the second, we are told of another shooting.
At Rafeef's school, one of the teachers, Abdel Raqeeb al-Obaidi, 45, takes us on to the rooftop to show us what he says are Houthi military camps, barracks and sniper positions in the mountains.
Standing on the rooftop, a Yemeni security adviser accompanying us suddenly tells us to go back inside. We are visible from these positions and could be shot, he says.
Abdel Raqeeb laughs, acknowledging the danger. He says the school has been fired on before.
"The situation may explode at any moment while we are sitting in class or sleeping or we are in school or we are out on the street. We do not know how our future is and how tomorrow is."
For Abdel Raqeeb, the risk has become routine. His familiarity with it is unsettling.
Taiz has long been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from the capital Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.
Seizing Taiz would give the Houthis full control over the country's north. Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.
Sometimes civilians are collateral damage in the fighting.
Later that evening, we get a call from a hospital about a five minute drive away from the school. Two children have been badly injured by a mortar strike.
When we arrive at Al-Rawdah Hospital, we see a nurse standing outside the intensive care unit, holding a tiny pair of beige, rubber sandals that are splattered with blood.
They belonged to Ahmed, a three-year-old boy who we learn was killed when a mortar struck a mechanic's shop in the city.
Shrapnel in the heart
When I ask about the shoes, the nurse, Ikram Shamsan, begins to cry.
"What did this child or his family ever do wrong?" she asks.
Ahmed was killed when a piece of shrapnel pierced his heart, entering through his back. The boy had been with his father, who was getting his motorcycle tyre pumped up at the mechanic's shop. The father was unharmed.
A doctor tells us the father had intended to leave his son at home, but the boy cried because he wanted to come too.
As he takes his son's body from the hospital, the father asks how he will face the boy's mother.
Completing a simple errand turned into the worst day of their lives.
Another boy, 11-year-old Amjad, was also at the mechanic's shop. He and his brother worked there with their uncle, sending money to their family in their home village.
Shrapnel has struck Amjad in his lung and abdomen. When we reach him, he is in intensive care, struggling to breathe. No relatives are beside his bed.
His doctor describes his condition as critical and fears he could die within hours. He hopes his mother will arrive in time to say goodbye.
Amjad was admitted at about 20:00 that evening. His mother reaches him at around 06:00 the following morning, delayed by the eight-hour journey from the village.
She sits beside his bed and prays, trying to remain composed. Once outside the room, she falls to her knees and breaks down.
Doctors say his heart rate improves during her visit. They judge him stable enough for another operation.
He has since undergone that surgery, but remains critically ill.
"We're always terrified. It's devastating to see children killed," says nurse Shamsan. "We want peace and we want to be safe."
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

bbc.com.title: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
bbc.com.text:
- Published
President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.
US media reports suggested that the decision was made due to intelligence suggesting that Iran was plotting a drone attack. The BBC has not confirmed this and Trump has refused to be drawn on the question.
The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.
One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.
Operation Spiderweb was an operation in June last year in which Ukraine smuggled drones into Russia. These were carried on lorries to locations near airbases by drivers who were unaware of their cargo, then launched and set upon their targets.
The source added: "Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously."
Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
While speaking to a group of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.
Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.
"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."
He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who - though later said "they would be linked to Iran" when asked.
The BBC has contacted the White House and the Ministry of Defence for comment.
Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world.
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Following the release of the first five men, Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.
He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."
Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident.
Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency.
However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added.
The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added.

bbc.com.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
bbc.com.text:
- Published
OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.
The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.
"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.
Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.
Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.
An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.
When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.
"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.
"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."
Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.
"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."
OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.
The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.
Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.
This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.
The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".
"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."
Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.
"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.
The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.
An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.
"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.
Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

bbc.com.title: Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.
On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goalscorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires on Tuesday (Wednesday 00:00 BST).
Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close - announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give.
Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.
His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to.
In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it.
Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.
Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game.
An owner who wants to be involved in everything
Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls.
And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner.
A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking.
An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything.
The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April.
CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD.
Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner.
The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention.
For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo".
The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him.
In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season.
A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga.
There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan.
Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed.
It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have.
Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona.
A growing business empire and love for youth football
Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup.
If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof.
He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams.
Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day.
This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others.
Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business.
His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017.
The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025.
MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection.
In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ángel Di María's property agency handling the sales.
He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels.
He has a mate collection with the drinkware giants Stanley, the brand's first multi-year deal with an athlete, and he gave his opinion on materials and colours.
The business side began with his father. Jorge Messi, who died in August aged 68, looked after his son's affairs from the start, and some of his early advice led the family into trouble with the tax authorities in Spain.
The company then grew into branches for TV production, marketing, media and commercial partnerships, among others, all well established by the time Jorge fell seriously ill.
Messi trusts the people who run them, some of them with him since his early days at Barcelona, and a thorough filter means he only gets offered and chooses what he is comfortable with.
He sets his own relationship with the business world, and nobody imposes anything on him.
In Miami last November, Messi told the America Business Forum: "Business is something that interests me. I would like to keep learning because I know nothing and I am just starting out."
The portfolio his circle has prepared is already impressive while he finds more football targets to keep the flame alive.

bbc.com.title: Watch: Moment Indonesian shoe shop is torn apart by explosion
bbc.com.text:
Watch: Moment Indonesian shoe shop is torn apart by explosion
CCTV has captured the moment a sports shoe shop was torn apart by an explosion in the San Antonio area of Surabaya, Indonesian authorities have confirmed.
Police said five people had been taken to hospital following the incident that was “strongly suspected” to be the result of a gas leak, and no suspicious substances or explosives were found at the site.
They added that at least 41 buildings had been damaged by the explosion.

bbc.com.title: Samoa leader apologises for Nazi salute after video from 2007 emerges
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Samoa's prime minister has apologised after a video emerged of him giving a Nazi salute while saying "Heil Hitler" at a family gathering.
In the seven-second clip filmed in July 2007, Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt is seen leading about a dozen people in the salute. "Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler!" he says, then thanks the group for responding.
Schmidt has acknowledged that his words and gesture "were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt", adding that the clip was recorded at a private gathering and "not intended for the public".
"I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism," Schmidt said in a statement published on Facebook on Monday.
The footage was first reported by local outlet the Samoa Observer in a news story on Sunday.
It said the video was filmed at a Schmidt family reunion in July 2007, when Schmidt was deputy speaker of parliament and quoted a family member who said he was the master of ceremonies at the gathering.
Samoa, a tiny island nation of about 221,000 people, sits about halfway between New Zealand and Hawaii.
It was under Germany's control in the early 20th century, but the colonisation ended shortly after World War One broke out.
Schmidt, who has Samoan and German heritage, took office as the country's eighth prime minister in September 2025.
He wore a Jewish prayer shawl during his swearing-in ceremony and has made clear his support for Israel during the early days of his premiership, saying that Samoa "stood with Israel".
"If people around the world don't like it, that's up to them, but Samoa stands with the land of God... There is only one God our country believes in, the God of Israel," he had said.

bbc.com.title: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Parnell said the secretary of the US Army would set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

bbc.com.title: What are the US midterms? A simple guide
bbc.com.text:
- Published
There are four weeks to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
What are the midterms?
On 3 November, Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.
A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.
The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.
The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.
Who is being elected?
All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. They serve fixed terms of two years. The House is commonly where proposed laws are introduced and debated.
Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs. Senators serve six-year terms. Among other jobs, they approve or block proposed laws that have been received from the House.
On the same day, voters across much of the US will also choose state-level politicians. Governor contests in California, Florida, Georgia and Michigan will be among the most closely watched.
What are the key issues?
The US economy is on the minds of many voters struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare.
Inflation remains above the level targeted by the US Federal Reserve, partly down to the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.
Democrats argue Trump's programme of trade tariffs have also pushed up prices for Americans.
Immigration is another key issue. Republicans say Trump has delivered on a major campaign pledge in 2024 by tightening the border and launching a widespread - and often controversial - crackdown on illegal immigration.
Concerns over AI have grown in urgency in recent weeks. Senior politicians from both parties have agreed on the need to regulate it - setting themselves in opposition to Trump, who has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology.
What is at stake?
Congress is one of the three branches of government, alongside the presidency and the judiciary. Control of it matters for the shaping of legislation.
Both the House and Senate are currently held by the Republican Party. But its majority is a slender one. They have 218 seats in the House, which is the minimum number needed to control it, plus one independent who votes with them. In the Senate, they have 53 seats and the minimum needed for control is 51.
If opposition Democrats win back control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor.
Who might win?
Voters have tended to "punish" the party of the president in the past and vote against them.
Recent polling shows a low approval rating for the president. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but in early October it was sitting at about 37%. Meanwhile 61% disapproved of him.
But not all seats in each chamber are competitive. Some are a safe bet for Republicans or Democrats.
The BBC's US partner CBS News has identified nine Senate races to watch, external, in states like Iowa and New Hampshire, and 42 House races, in states like Arizona and Ohio.
The vote is more unpredictable this year because of a battle between the two parties over the way voting districts in the House of Representatives are drawn.
Republicans tried to gain an advantage by creating more favourable electoral maps in certain states and Democrats followed suit.
What does it mean for Trump?
If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get any laws through Congress.
So his domestic plans could be frustrated, although he has found ways to exercise power without his wider party.
Democratic control of either chamber would also mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. Corruption allegations, the new White House ballroom and ICE tactics could be subject to scrutiny.
There is also a debate within the Democratic Party about whether to impeach Trump, which means to bring charges in Congress that will form the basis for a political, not criminal, trial.
If the Republican Party stays in control of Congress, Trump will be able to keep going with his plans for the remainder of his time in office.
What does it mean for the 2028 election?
The president's name is not on the ballot during the midterm elections, though Trump has urged Republicans to pretend that it is by voting for him as an endorsement of his actions so far.
Whichever way the results fall, commentators are likely to use them to make arguments about how voters feel about the direction of the country under Trump's leadership.
Trump cannot run to be president a third time. After the midterms, we can expect speculation to start building about who might be his successor as the Republican presidential nominee for 2028 - and who might compete against that person for the Democrats.
Additional reporting by Deirdre Finnerty

bbc.com.title: Five reasons India's stock market is sinking even when its economy is growing
bbc.com.text:
- Published
India's economy is growing at an enviable rate of over 7% despite global energy shocks, rising interest rates, tariff uncertainties and weather-related disruptions.
But the world's fastest growing major economy also has one of the worst performing major equity markets in 2026. The correction in Indian stocks has, in fact, only intensified in recent weeks.
The benchmark Sensex and Nifty indices, which represent the country's largest companies, have inched up slightly since Monday after posting losses for eight straight weeks - the longest losing streak in 25 years, according to Reuters.
Indian mom-and-pop investors who put their money into the Nifty have seen their wealth erode by about 15% this year. In comparison, they would have made 62% returns on Korea's Kospi index since January or 170% in the last two years.
On aggregate, the money foreign investors have put into Indian markets in the past decade - after subtracting what they sold or withdrew - is nearing zero. In the past two years alone, foreign institutional investors have withdrawn a staggering $40bn, according to data from Bernstein Research.
It is the large pool of domestic institutional and retail money, flowing into instruments like mutual funds, that have helped the markets avoid a sharper fall.
Domestic assets under management of mutual funds have grown from about $125bn in 2016 to some $900bn this year, with the number of Indians parking money in stocks and mutual funds more than tripling to 150 million individuals.
This makes the recent fall in the markets more worrying - since households, already struggling from a weak job market, high inflation and faltering consumption, are now seeing their equity savings take a beating too.
So, what's gone wrong?
Here are five reasons India's booming economy isn't lifting its stock market.
Persistent energy shocks due to Middle East conflict
Crude oil prices have hovered between $90 and $100 a barrel as the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz enters its eighth month, far longer than analysts had expected. Moreover, there's little visibility on when normalcy will return.
"This single variable tends to influence the markets quite negatively," Hari Shyamsunder, a fund manager with Franklin Templeton Asset Management India, told the BBC. "Markets can absorb crude between $70 and $90, but when prices move above $100 a barrel, it starts putting stress on macro-economic variables such as inflation and also company earnings and margins."
India imports over 90% of its requirements - nearly half of its crude oil imports, along with a large share of its liquified petroleum gas (LPG) and liquified natural gas (LNG) shipments, come through the Strait of Hormuz.
While Delhi has diversified its energy sources, tapping Russian oil markets, US President Donald Trump recently threatened up to 100% tariffs on countries doing trade with Moscow, further complicating matters.
Rising global interest rates
With oil prices rising, inflation is going up and, as a result, interest rates are on the rise globally. The effective yield on US government bonds is above 5%, or at near 25-year highs.
These are often considered risk-free investments. As a result, foreign money tends to leave riskier emerging market assets such as Indian equities and chase safer investments like US bonds when interest rates rise.
Falling rupee
For foreign investors, the problem of muted returns has been compounded by a weaker rupee. In currency-adjusted dollar terms, they have suffered because of the fall in the Indian currency.
The Nifty has delivered just 6% annualised dollar returns over the past decade - hardly attractive, especially in comparison with several other competing markets.
Indian stocks are cheaper, but still relatively expensive
Stock valuations have been another major concern.
The market correction over the last two years has reduced the premium that Indian stocks held over their emerging market competitors.
"Stocks are cheaper than they have been on average for the last ten years," says Shyamsunder, adding that the premium that Indian shares commanded over other emerging economies has shrunk substantially in the past few years.
However, they are still expensive relative to their earnings, especially since companies in countries such as South Korea and Taiwan have benefited from a huge boom in artificial intelligence (AI) which has pushed up their profits.
The missing AI piece
In India, AI, or the new economy broadly, is a major missing piece of its growth story.
"Many of India's large caps [big companies] represent a bygone economic era," Bernstein Research said in a note recently. "Most are not investing in the future, but consolidating their past, often expecting policy to continue shielding them from global competition."
And its smaller companies are yet to reach a scale that will attract foreign institutional funds.
While Indian companies are investing in data centres and chip fabrication, the country has not produced a global giant like OpenAI, Anthropic or even China's DeepSeek - this is where the largest share of the profits in the AI value chain lie.
Foreign investor interest will only return to India meaningfully if it can build globally competitive industries in these emerging areas, according to Bernstein.
"We are seeing early signs of this in areas such as space, defence, semiconductors, and deep-tech innovation, but most remain too small to materially influence capital allocation decisions over much of this decade."
So what's next?
There are many immediate factors that will influence how Indian markets behave going forward.
"Easing geopolitical tensions and relatively attractive valuations could support a revival in FPI [foreign portfolio investor] inflows," according to CareEdge, a brokerage, though trade tensions and higher energy prices remain a “challenge for corporate performance going ahead”.
To what extent corporate margins have been squeezed will become clearer as they start reporting quarterly earnings from this week.
For now, while foreign investors may have given up, Indian savers, even though increasingly more anxious, haven't slowed their monthly investment flows , externalinto mutual funds.
The real test will be whether this resilience survives a deeper correction in the future.

bbc.com.title: Blue Planet and Gandhi composer George Fenton dies aged 76
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Composer George Fenton, whose work included music for films such as Gandhi, Groundhog Day and The Fisher King, as well as TV shows like Planet Earth and Bergerac, has died at the age of 76.
The prolific musician received five Oscar nominations for his film scores, including those for Dangerous Liasions and Cry Freedom.
His work on the BBC TV show Blue Planet also earned awards from the Baftas, Emmy Awards and Ivor Novellos; and he also composed theme music for BBC News programmes such as Newsnight and Breakfast Time.
In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today."
They continued: "He is survived by his loving wife Amanda, ex-wife Jane, children Gemma, Grace and Bridget, and grandchildren Lola, Audrey, Alfred, George, Frank and Beatrice, and a life of music."
The cause of death was not disclosed but, underlining the suddenness of his passing, Fenton had signed a new worldwide publishing deal just three weeks ago, external.
At the time, he said he was working on two new film scores and a musical.
Fenton was born George Howe in Bromley, Kent in 1949. According to a biography on his official website, external, his father was a mechanical engineer, and his mother had been a dancer before becoming a nurse during the war.
Both parents were musical - his father played drums and his mother played piano - but Fenton chose the electric guitar as his instrument at the age of seven.
That was "when music became more important than football," he later told The Express newspaper, external. "The Beatles had a huge influence on me."
He took his first lessons from a musician called Brian Rudd.
"He came into our lives as a chimney sweep, which he clearly wasn't," Fenton later recalled.
"My mother went mad at him because he filled the house with soot.
"As he left he said, 'I'm really sorry – but I tuned the boy's guitar for you.' She suggested that as compensation for the mess he could give me a lesson, which he did and then carried on doing."
Later, Fenton began to study the church organ, but rejected the offer of music college to pursue a stage career.
In 1968, he appeared in Alan Bennett's first West End play Forty Years On. Upon joining the actor's union Equity, he was forced to adopt his mother's maiden name, due to rules preventing two actors from sharing the same name.
During that production, he also understudied the musical director of the show, Carl Davis - who also became a prominent composer for film and television.
A year later, Fenton signed a record deal, and scored a top 10 hit in Sweden with a cover of The Beatles' Maxwell's Silver Hammer, external, but his career as a solo artist was short lived.
In the mid-1970s, he took a recurring role as the soldier Martin Gimbel in the ITV soap opera Emmerdale Farm.
But as time went on, he found that directors were always casting him in roles that required him to play an instrument, so he decided to make music his main focus.
Fenton got his first job as composer and musical director for a production of Twelfth Night at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1974.
Eight years later, he was nominated for an Oscar for his score for Richard Attenborough's Gandhi, external, on which he worked with Indian composer and instrumentalist Ravi Shankar to develop themes reflecting the country's musical traditions.
It was only his fourth attempt at film music, and he was still almost entirely self-taught.
Throughout the 1980s, he wrote the soundtrack for a number of TV series, including the Bafta-winning The Jewel in the Crown, The Monocled Mutineer, and Alan Bennett's Talking Heads.
He also wrote many well-known theme tunes, including the BBC's One O'Clock News, Six O'Clock News, Nine O'Clock News, Newsnight, The Money Programme, and Radio 4's PM Programme.
For 1987's Cry Freedom - the story of South African campaigner Steve Biko, who was brutally killed by police - he worked with South African jazz musician Jonas Gwangwa, earning two Oscar nominations for best original score and song.
Almost by accident, the title track featured Fenton singing, external a list of anti-apartheid activists imprisoned or killed by the South African government.
He'd initially recorded the lyrics as a guide for Gwangwa - but the musician decided to keep some of them intact "as a gesture of brotherhood".
"Then it got nominated for an Oscar, so I then found myself singing it on live television to about a billion people, which was not what I intended at all," Fenton later told Radio 4's Desert Island Discs.
After composing the score for the BBC's Trials of Life in 1990, Fenton went on to create the music for what became known as David Attenborough's Earth Trilogy: The Blue Planet, external, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet.
Fenton's music perfectly complemented the stunning visuals of the ocean's depths and the polar ice caps, adding an emotional weight to the narrative, using the full might of the orchestra to evoke everything from wonder and awe to tension and suspense.
Following the success of the documentaries, Fenton created a show - The Blue Planet in Concert - which has been performed by leading orchestras in venues around the world.
Among his other well-known soundtracks were The Long Walk Home, You've Got Mail, Sweet Home Alabama, The Lady In The Van and Mrs Henderson Presents.
Fenton also scored more films for British director Ken Loach than any other composer.
Their 18 collaborations included Ladybird, Ladybird; I, Daniel Blake and The Wind That Shakes the Barley, which won the Palme d'Or at the 2006 Cannes Film Festival.
He also founded the Association of Professional Composers, which later merged with The Ivors Academy; and he is one of only a handful of musicians to receive the Academy's fellowship, alongside Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber, Sir Elton John, Kate Bush, Bruce Springsteen and George Michael.
In addition, Fenton was a visiting professor at the Royal College of Music and the University of Nottingham. He was made a CBE for services to music in 2023.
The composer often said that his musical career had been an accident, but nothing gave him greater joy than seeing his work come to life.
On his episode of Desert Island Discs, Fenton chose one of his own compositions - Reunion, from the soundtrack to the movie Accidental Hero - as it reminded him of watching pianist John Lowe play the melody in the studio.
"If I was sitting on a desert island and thinking about what a good time I'd had writing music, which I have, I want just one thing to remind me about the best part - which is the fact that you write something and then you're so surprised and thrilled at the way it's played," he told Sue Lawley.
"For a composer, that's the biggest kick you can get."

bbc.com.title: Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
bbc.com.text:
- Published
"I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."
Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.
The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.
However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.
Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.
Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.
During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.
Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshot and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.
His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials.
"People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, told BBC Sinhala.
The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.
Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.
The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.
His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.
The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.
In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers.
"There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, President's Counsel, told BBC Sinhala.
Back home, communication between Anojan and his family has completely ceased.
"My brother hasn't called for two days." Hamsidan said on 28 September. "We informed the embassy and asked officials to look into the matter and update us. They said they would check. We are still waiting, as we have not yet received a response."
In Saudi prisons, inmates on death row typically lose access to personal mobile devices, with formal calls strictly facilitated through prison authorities.
Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns regarding severe sentences for online speech in Saudi Arabia.
In July 2023, Mohammed Al Ghamdi, a retired Saudi school teacher, was sentenced to death over his comments on multiple social media platforms, according to the United Nations.
"The death sentence against Mohammad bin Nasser al-Ghamdi, who has a total of just 10 followers on both of his anonymous Twitter accounts and is accused of nothing other than expressing his opinions on social media, is ludicrous," Philip Luther, Amnesty International's Research and Advocacy Director for the Middle East and North Africa, said at the time.
Al Ghamdi's ruling was overturned, and he was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to ALQST for human rights, an independent non-governmental organisation defending and promoting human rights in Saudi Arabia.
There are more than 10 million foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). Rights groups emphasise that low-wage migrant workers face distinct vulnerabilities in the Saudi legal system due to language barriers and lack of proper legal representation.
Executions for blasphemy are relatively rare compared with those for drug offences or murder handed down by courts in Saudi Arabia.

aljazeera.com.title: Tennis: World number one Sinner will not play in 2026 due to knee injury
aljazeera.com.text:
World number one men’s tennis player Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery from a knee injury that has kept him out of action since his triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.
The five-time Grand Slam winner will “follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee”, Sinner’s team said in a statement on Tuesday.
“The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027. As a result, Jannik will be unable to compete again during the 2026 season.”
Sinner also posted the update on his personal Instagram account, where he recounted ending last year on a high after retaining his ATP Finals title in Turin as he battled past then world number one Carlos Alcaraz.
“But at the moment, I also need to think about my long-term career,” he said in a video posted on Instagram.
“I will do everything possible to get back to 100 percent [and] I hope to see you very, very soon on court again.”
Sinner, 25, has not played since his triumph at the All England Club, missing the North American hardcourt swing, including the US Open, and the ongoing ATP 500 event in Beijing.
He announced last week that he was withdrawing from the Shanghai Masters, which he won in 2024 after defeating Novak Djokovic in the final.
Now he will also miss the Paris Masters and the ATP Finals in November. Plus, he will not be able to play for Italy, the host nation and three-time defending champion, in the Davis Cup Final 8.
Sinner risks losing the top ranking while he’s out.
But if Sinner does return at the start of next year, he could play the Australian Open – the next Grand Slam – which starts January 17.
He enjoyed a 30-match winning streak this year before his meltdown in a second-round defeat at the French Open amid a Paris heatwave.
Sinner’s main rival missed four and a half months this year due to a right wrist injury.
Meanwhile, Germany’s Alexander Zverev won two of the four Grand Slam titles and is nearing the No 1 ranking.

aljazeera.com.title: How Palestinian reporters defied Israel’s genocide to redefine journalism
aljazeera.com.text:
Israel has killed about 250 journalists since launching its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023. That is more than the number of journalists killed in all wars in the past 150 years combined.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) says Israel has engaged in “the deadliest and most deliberate effort to kill and silence journalists” that the media watchdog has ever documented.
Jonathan Dagher, the head of Reporters Without Borders’ Middle East desk, called the targeting of journalists “a tragedy for journalism”, while the United Nations human rights chief, Volker Turk, called Gaza “a ‘death trap’ for journalists”.
Yet, beyond the statements and condolences, Israel has never been held accountable for its killing of Palestinian journalists – a practice that long predates the genocidal war on Gaza, but that took on an industrial scale over the past three years.
Instead, the silence of the international community and lack of solidarity from Western media professionals emboldened Israel as it pursued the genocidal war and normalised journalists’ killings.
But despite trying to suppress the truth about its massacres and attempts at ethnic cleansing, Israel – historically an acknowledged master at propaganda – has largely failed in its efforts over the past three years, thanks to the bravery of the very voices it tried to silence.
That too is the story of how journalism has changed since October 7, 2023.
‘Neutral’ amid genocide
Western media outlets and their prominent faces often claimed to be “neutral” in their coverage of the genocidal war.
But the very concept of neutrality in journalism has come under question amid the genocide.
The Western media were rarely neutral when viewed according to the basic tenets of journalism and professional standards. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza so far. But Western outlets often framed headlines in the passive tense when reporting on these killings, conveniently shielding Israel from blame.
Palestinians were killed by Israel, mostly in circumstances that violated rules of war. These details were not highlighted, and the Israeli narrative that Hamas was using Palestinian civilians as a “human shield” was amplified.
When Al Jazeera journalist Anas al-Sharif was killed in a targeted attack in front of al-Shifa Hospital in August 2025, CNN carried the Israeli accusation that he worked for a Hamas cell in its second paragraph, an allegation Al Jazeera has rejected.
Weeks before the killing, Irene Khan, the UN’s special rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression, had warned against “repeated threats and accusations” against al-Sharif by the Israeli army.
Israel killed 22 people, including five journalists – one of whom worked for Al Jazeera – in a “double-tap” strike in September 2025. It claimed that it had targeted a “Hamas camera.” Most media outlets ran the story. The Reuters news agency, whose journalist was also killed in the attack, confirmed that the camera belonged to it.
Similarly, when Israel targeted media personnel in Lebanon early in the war, a Sky News post on X called it a hit on a “Hezbollah-linked” broadcaster.
Israel has also been accused of jailing and torturing Palestinian journalists for doing their job. During the genocidal war, it has tried to control the narrative domestically too, cracking down on Haaretz for its critical coverage of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s failures on October 7, 2023, and the atrocities in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The Netanyahu government imposed a ban on Al Jazeera, calling the network a security threat. Al Jazeera described the shutdown as a “criminal act” and warned that Israel’s suppression of the free press “stands in contravention of international and humanitarian law”.
This was not the first time Al Jazeera has been targeted. In 2021, a Gaza building housing Al Jazeera’s office was destroyed in an Israeli missile strike. Israel has killed many Al Jazeera journalists even before October 2023.
Shireen Abu Akleh, considered a voice of Palestine, was killed by an Israeli soldier while she was reporting in the occupied West Bank in 2022. Her killer was never charged for the murder.
Assal Rad, an activist and Middle East historian, has accused the Western media of enabling attacks on journalists.
“When you’re repeating what Israel says, you’re creating space to legitimise the targeting of their own colleagues,” she said in an interview with Columbia Journalism Review on September 30.
Double standards
While reporting on Russian aggression against Ukraine, media around the world rightly humanised the victims.
But that same journalistic standard was missing, far too often, when Western outlets reported on Palestinians killed by Israel. Instead, they were at times portrayed as collateral damage, their deaths the result of fighting between two sides.
Israel has killed more than 21,000 children in Gaza in the last three years. But the faces of thousands of babies, children and mothers, and their suffering and despair, were frequently buried under statistics. They were nameless, faceless, their lives and stories deemed unworthy of human treatment.
Moreover, Western reporting often lacked historical contextualisation, erasing the history of Israel’s brutal occupation, territorial expansion and the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. More than 750,000 Palestinians were expelled or displaced from their homes, leading up to the formation of Israel in 1948. Israel has since forcibly displaced more Palestinians from the occupied territory.
Israeli leaders now publicly oppose the establishment of Palestinian statehood as part of the so-called two-state solution and successive governments have expanded illegal settlements on Palestinian lands.
Western media often present settler violence and government-backed illegal settlement expansion as separate, when in fact, the Israeli government has armed, funded and granted impunity to those involved.
Fundamentally, treating Israel – an occupying power in Gaza and the West Bank – and Palestinians as equal sides is itself problematic. It is not objective journalism; it is far from it. It misses the asymmetry inherent in this equation. On the one hand is a major military power in illegal occupation of another people’s land, waging a genocidal war on them and seeking to ethnically cleanse them; on the other is a Palestinian resistance movement consisting of multiple strands united only in their struggle to achieve self-determination, a right guaranteed under the UN Charter.
Objectivity requires that news reports highlight Israel’s use of disproportionate force and the firing of banned weapons at civilian areas – violations of the rules of war and war crimes. Instead, Palestinian experts and commentators were the ones grilled and pressed to condemn Hamas as a condition for even being heard.
The challenge
Still, the Western media’s lopsided coverage did not go unchallenged. It triggered rebellion in several newsrooms, including the BBC and The New York Times.
More than 1,500 Western journalists from various news organisations signed an open letter in protest against the coverage of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Eight BBC journalists wrote an open letter, accusing the broadcaster of failing to accurately report on the Israel-Palestine conflict.
They accused their organisation of running with pro-Israel editorial biases, downplaying Palestinian casualties and suppressing terms like “genocide”, “apartheid” or “occupation”. Many journalists of colour resigned in protest.
This has dented the credibility of Western media’s reporting on critical international issues at a time of global upheaval.
However, the unprecedented Israeli attacks on journalists did not deter Palestinians from reporting. They risked their lives to get the story out via social media, especially TikTok and Instagram.
“They take revenge on us through our children? It doesn’t matter. We will stay. We will continue. This is our path, and we chose it knowingly. We will not stop,” said Wael al-Dahdouh, Al Jazeera Arabic’s then-Gaza bureau chief, after Israel killed his wife, daughter, two sons, and a grandson in separate Israeli air strikes.
People across the world, including young Americans who primarily consume news on social media, were horrified by the graphic images coming out of Palestine despite the efforts of legacy media outlets to sanitise the Gaza genocide.
It triggered student protests at Columbia University that soon spread to other campuses.
Palestinian journalists became “the eyes of Gaza”, showing the world what rights organisations dubbed Israel’s “livestreamed genocide” against Palestinians.
One of them, Bisan Owda, who won an Emmy Award for her reporting on daily life and survival during the genocidal war on Gaza, is known for her resilience as a Palestinian journalist.
“Hello, my name is Bisan, and I am still alive…” became Owda’s signature greeting in her social media posts.
“I no longer have any dreams. My only dream is to survive this, to tell the story of the people who didn’t,” she said on the 27th day of the genocidal war.
She and hundreds of Palestinian journalists have done just that. In the process, they have upended a media landscape where giant organisations beholden to power have long controlled who gets to be heard and seen.
Ultimately, Israel’s genocide in Gaza has also been a war on truth. Thanks to Owda and her Palestinian colleagues, that is a war Israel has lost.

aljazeera.com.title: Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried?
aljazeera.com.text:
Dozens of people have been quarantined in Russia’s Siberia after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances.
Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported the woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube and died.
Plague is a severe, life-threatening infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Between 1346 and 1353, the bubonic plague – one of three forms of the disease – was known as the Black Death. It caused one of the most fatal pandemics in the world across Eurasia and North Africa. Some 30-60 percent of the population of Europe is believed to have died in that outbreak.
Pneumonic plague is less common than bubonic plague. It is a severe form of the infection that can spread from person to person.
What happened in the Russian lab and should we be worried?
Here’s what we know:
What happened in the Russian lab?
On Monday, Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague last week.
According to some Russian media reports, Shipilova became ill while at work on September 30 and died two days later at a hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov. A number of media reports suggest there may have been an accident at the lab, but this has not been officially confirmed.
About 200 people who came into contact with the dead woman have since been quarantined, and parts of the hospital where she died have also been cordoned off. An aluminium plant nearby has instructed its workers to wear masks.
Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk to meet with Governor Igor Kobzev and other officials four days ago.
In a statement quoted by the TASS news agency, Rospotrebnadzor said officials in Irkutsk region had, however, detected two cases of COVID and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with the researcher. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted.
Later on Monday, Russian authorities said they found no evidence that the woman’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with and said the situation was under control.
Kobzev said in a statement that the woman had died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, adding: “Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified.”
He added that the situation was under control and that all known contacts with the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.
What is plague and what are its symptoms?
The bacterium which causes plague, Yersinia pestis, is carried by small wild mammals and their fleas. In Siberia, where it is endemic, it is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, however, though cases occur every year in other parts of the world, notably in Africa.
According to the Centres for Disease Control (CDC) in the US, plague has been detected in people of all ages, from babies to those aged in their 90s. Half of cases occur in people aged from 12 to 45. Men and women are both susceptible, although historically it has been slightly more common among men.
There are three main types of plague, affecting different parts of the body. These are bubonic, septicaemic and pneumonic. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), bubonic plague is the most common clinical form. Symptoms include painful swollen lymph nodes or “buboes”.
Septicaemic plague infects the blood while pneumonic plague affects the lungs.
The WHO describes septicaemic and pneumonic plague as “less common, but severe forms” of plague.
A fourth type, pharyngeal plague, is rare. It can be contracted by eating infected meat.
According to the US-based Cleveland Clinic, besides swollen lymph nodes in the case of bubonic plague, those infected can display the following symptoms:
- Fever and chills.
- Headaches and body aches.
- Weakness and fatigue.
- Dizziness.
- Nausea.
- Vomiting and diarrhoea.
Complications can arise from plague if it is untreated, according to the Cleveland Clinic. These include:
- Meningitis – a severe infection which causes the inflammation of the lining of the brain and spinal cord.
- Tissue death and loss of limbs from gangrene.
- Respiratory failure.
- Organ failure.
Bubonic plague has a fatality rate of 30 percent to 60 percent. Pneumonic and septicaemic plague are both fatal if left untreated within one to six days, the WHO says.
If identified quickly, however, all forms can be treated with antibiotics.
How does plague spread?
Plague most commonly spreads through the bites of fleas carried by rodents, but can also be transmitted from person to person.
According to the CDC in the US, people can also become infected through exposure to sick pets, especially cats.
These are the main ways the disease can be transmitted:
Flea bites
According to the CDC, people and animals can contract plague from dead rats carrying the disease as well as being bitten by fleas which have bitten infected rats. “Dogs and cats may also bring plague-infected fleas into the home. Flea bite exposure may result in primary bubonic plague or septicemic plague,” the CDC states.
Direct contact
Humans can contract plague through contact with the tissue or body fluids of an infected animal. This form of exposure most commonly results in bubonic plague or septicaemic plague, according to the CDC.
Infectious droplets
Droplets coughed out by humans and animals infected with pneumonic plague can hang in the air and be inhaled by another person. The CDC states that this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague, and it is the only way the disease can be transmitted from person to person.
According to the CDC, the last documented case of person-to-person pneumonic plague transmission was in 1924. However, there have been more recent cases of pneumonic plague transmitted to humans by sick cats.
“Cats are particularly susceptible to plague and can be infected by eating infected rodents. Cats with plague pose a risk of transmitting infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians,” the CDC states.
Where does plague exist?
Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, told The Associated Press news agency that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia”.
Worldwide, there are between 1,000 and 2,000 cases of plague every year, according to the Cleveland Clinic in the US.
Plague is endemic to Siberia, which is the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak. Besides Russia, plague is also endemic in several other countries, according to the WHO. Between 2019 and 2025, the majority of new cases recorded by WHO occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.
There have been rare cases elsewhere. In July 2025, Arizona a man who worked with cats died from pneumonic plague – the first such death since 2007.
There was a major outbreak of bubonic plague in Los Angeles1924 to 1925 after it was first recorded in the US in 1900, brought by infected rates in steamships. Bubonic plague has made up 80 percent of an average of seven cases per year in the US since then. Most of these have occurred in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and western Nevada, according to the CDC.
Why has this incident triggered global alarm?
While authorities in Russia have stressed that postmortem tests carried out on the woman did not detect that she had plague, the incident has raised global alarm.
