aljazeera.com.title: Gauff in racial abuse controversy at China Open after replayed point
aljazeera.com.text:
Coco Gauff says she has received an “insane” amount of racial abuse on social media after the two-time Grand Slam champion beat local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open in a third-round match, where a replayed point prompted an online backlash.
The American tennis star won 7-5, 6-1 to reach the fourth round, but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set, raising her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner.
After a video review, the umpire ordered a replay. Gauff won the replayed point and held serve for 5-5 before cruising to victory against the 16-year-old Chinese.
Gauff said she had received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match.
“You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist,” Gauff, who is Black, said on X early on Tuesday in reply to a post containing a racial slur.
“The amount of racist comments/direct messages I’ve received in the last few hours is insane.
“Lastly, I’m not a cheater or a thief.”
The WTA has made efforts to tackle the issue of online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system which monitors thousands of players and officials on social media.
A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to more than 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier.
Gauff also explained that she was following the rules when she challenged the point. Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgement calls, including claims a distraction may have interfered with play.
The 22-year-old said she had spoken to Sun about the point at the end of the match.
“Xinran’s an incredible talent and player, I apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood,” she wrote.
“I didn’t like to see her so emotional as I’ve been there and I really understand what it’s like but this is the beginning of an incredible career. It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd.”

npr.org.title: What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes
npr.org.text:
What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes
NEW DELHI — Protests have spread across India in the past week as opposition parties and civil society groups demand the resignation of the country's election chief over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
The campaign has been led in part by India's "Cockroach" youth movement, which previously organized street protests that forced the education minister to resign in July.
Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the poll body's ongoing revision of voter lists. They accuse the revision could disenfranchise millions of voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP. The commission and government deny any wrongdoing.
Here's what to know:
Voter list changes fueling the protests
India is the world's largest democracy with hundreds of millions of people voting in national and state elections. The Election Commission plays a central role in determining voter eligibility and administering elections, making changes to electoral lists politically significant.
The dispute centers on a nationwide voter list revision known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. It began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of local elections and has since expanded to most of India's states and federally administered territories.
Under the process, voters are required to provide documents showing they are eligible to remain on the lists.
The Election Commission says the exercise is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and ensure legitimate voters remain registered. Critics say it could instead exclude legitimate voters, particularly poorer and other vulnerable communities.
They also say the requirements are confusing and difficult for many people to provide, particularly those who lack older government records or other documents.
Critics say the changes could benefit Modi's party
India's Election Commission is an independent constitutional body overseeing elections and maintaining voter lists, but opposition parties accuse the commission of favoring Modi's party. They allege the changes could remove people more likely to support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters who favor the BJP.
The BJP and the Election Commission reject the allegations and say the revision has no political motive. Modi's party says the list is being updated to weed out what they call "infiltrators."
The issue was prominent in West Bengal's crucial state elections earlier this year after a voter list revision removed about 9 million names, or roughly 12% of the electorate. The deletions left millions of eligible voters unable to cast ballots. Modi's party won the state for the first time.
Politics can impact commission rulings
Indian law requires a majority vote of commission members to enact changes making disagreements among its members potentially significant.
The Indian Express newspaper reported in September that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems.
The newspaper reported Kumar, the election chief, rejected those objections.
The Election Commission said the report reflected "differing views and deliberations" rather than formal written objections.
Protesters seek end to changes that could reshape elections
The "Cockroach" movement, opposition parties and civil society groups have called for Kumar to resign or be removed and for an inquiry into his conduct, including possible criminal proceedings. They want the current revision halted and the previous electoral lists used for future elections.
They also demand a more independent and transparent process for appointing election commissioners.
Election Commission data indicates voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30%, fueling concerns among opposition parties and protest groups over potential exclusions.
The dispute is likely to intensify as the changes resulting from the revision expand throughout India, which is facing a series of state elections early next year.

npr.org.title: Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat
npr.org.text:
Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat
HANOI, Vietnam — Police in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said.
Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others were being investigated for theft, state media said Monday.
Investigators said Binh bought stolen cats, kept them at a facility in the city's north and resold them for meat. He worked with suppliers who recruited others to ride motorcycles through residential neighborhoods between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., hunting for cats and trapping four to 10 cats each night.
Eating dog and cat meat is not unique to Vietnam and has been practiced in parts of Asia, though it is not common practice. In Vietnam, cat meat traditionally is more commonly consumed in the north, among older generations.
The practice has declined with growing pet ownership and urbanization, and younger Vietnamese are more likely to regard dogs and cats as companion animals.
In 2024, more than 250,000 people signed a petition calling for an end to Vietnam's dog and cat meat trade. The city of Hoi An also pledged in 2021 to end the sale and consumption of dog and cat meat.
Some believe eating cat meat brings good luck, though there is no scientific evidence for such claims.
Police raided the network on July 8 and found about 50 cats and dozens of traps, state media reported.
The suspects told investigators they had stolen and sold about 2,700 cats, the reports said. Police did not say how long the operation had been running.
Police returned 13 of the cats confiscated in the raid to their owners. A nonprofit animal rights group was caring for the others while authorities sought to identify their owners.
Under Vietnamese law, dogs and cats are considered private property, and stealing them is considered theft. Criminal prosecution generally applies when the value of the stolen property exceeds 2 million dong ($77).
In a separate raid in June, police reported they had rescued more than 400 cats. At least 40 were reunited with their owners, but dozens of dead cats were found packed in ice.

npr.org.title: Ex-spy chief is arrested in Germany on suspicion of trading state secrets and treason
npr.org.text:
Ex-spy chief is arrested in Germany on suspicion of trading state secrets and treason
BERLIN — A former head of Germany 's foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor's office said.
August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is "strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage," the federal prosecutor's office said in a statement.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for.
The premises of both men were searched Tuesday.
Former aide allegedly supplied Hanning with BND documents
The prosecutor's office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning's chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
"In his role, he had access to confidential information," the prosecutor's office said.
Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said.
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings," the statement said.
Hanning used the information in private consulting work, and on one occasion "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service."
Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information for several years, the statement said, but it was not immediately clear if the collaboration continued until their arrests on Tuesday.
The office did not say which country the foreign agent worked for and said "it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient."
The statement added that "Hanning was in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years."
Hanning is suspected of involvement in a prominent child abduction case
Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block's children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years.
The investigation into that case led to Tuesday's arrests.
The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning's residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor's office stated.
Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from Block in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor's office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa.
The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain Block House. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court.
A message to the BND for comment was not immediately returned.
German opposition lawmaker calls for a quick probe
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
"This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story," said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
"We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations leveled against former BND chief Hanning," von Notz told Spiegel Online.
"We have been criticizing the dubious and wide-ranging lobbying activities of former top officials and those with the highest security clearances in the Germany for years," he said and called for banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office, Spiegel Online reported.

npr.org.title: Dems have edge in midterms, poll shows. And, Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to close
npr.org.text:
Dems have edge in midterms, poll shows. And, Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to close
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
In four weeks, Election Day will be here, and a series of new polls show Democrats have a decided advantage in the midterms. They are favored to win the House with a narrow majority. Democrats need 218 seats for a majority, and the Cook Political Report forecasts a net gain of five to 15 seats, which would give them between 220 and 230 seats in January. The Senate has shifted more dramatically. Six seats have moved toward the Democrats' direction since June, according to Cook's ratings. Initially seen as a long shot for Democrats, the Senate is now within reach. These projections come as President Trump's approval rating is low.
- 🎧 Polls are just one factor to consider for the midterms, NPR's Domenico Montanaro tells Up First. He notes that people should consider the importance of history, the national environment, political structure and money as factors as well. And people still have to vote in the elections, but even so, the momentum seems to be shifting toward Democrats, particularly in the Senate. Democratic gains in the House are uncertain, as the party's unpopularity and the fact that 25 of the 31 targeted districts are in areas Trump won in 2024 could make it hard to tip the scales in their favor, Montanaro says.
- ➡️ If you haven't registered to vote yet, it isn't too late. Here's what you need to know about registration in your state.
- ➡️ Find the latest election news from NPR and your local station on the NPR app.
A new era in Hollywood is set to arrive today as David Ellison's long-anticipated $111 billion merger with Paramount-Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery is expected to close. Despite facing months of public protests, the deal has cleared legal and regulatory challenges in the U.S. and Europe. The media conglomerate Skydance unites two film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, both more than 100 years old.
- 🎧 Ellison defended the merger against critics concerned about him having too much media power, NPR's Mandalit del Barco says. As part of a settlement to move the deal forward, Ellison agreed to produce 30 films a year with the combined studios, but critics remain skeptical. Concerns also linger about CNN's future, given that Ellison is an ally of Trump. To address these worries, Ellison promised to establish an independent oversight board to protect CNN from political interference. People who don't agree with the deal predict that viewers may soon see an increase in cost for streaming services and they could have fewer choices, according to del Barco.
Catherine Sweeney from NPR network station WPLN was one of seven media witnesses to observe Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike, the first woman to face the death penalty in the state in nearly 200 years. Each witness sensed that the lethal injection might not proceed smoothly. Pike's attorneys had requested the Tennessee Supreme Court to allow hanging instead due to concerns that her platelet disorder and small veins would make the injection painful and ineffective. Sweeney describes what she saw and heard throughout that day.
Russian authorities are urging people to remain calm after a worker at an infectious diseases institute in Siberia died from a mysterious illness, raising speculation about a potential plague outbreak. Last Tuesday, a 28-year-old female lab worker at the anti-plague Research Institute in Irkutsk fell ill and died two days later. Questions remain over the cause of her death. Here's what we do and don't know.
On the road to the midterms
by Majd Al-Waheidi, Morning Edition and Up First digital editor
Four weeks from now, the midterm election will help decide the balance of power in Congress. And ahead of Election Day, Morning Edition will be traveling to six states with some of the most competitive races to hear what voters say is shaping their decisions.
Steve Inskeep is reporting from North Carolina and Georgia. Michel Martin is headed to Ohio and Michigan. Leila Fadel is reporting from Maine. And A Martínez is heading to Texas.
Across the political divide, one concern keeps rising to the top: the cost of living and what it means for people's economic futures.
But voters are weighing more than their bills. Immigration and the rapid growth of massive data centers are also part of the conversation. So is the voting process itself, including new restrictions that are raising questions about how ballots will be cast, secured and counted.
Over the next four weeks, Morning Edition will report from different races and electorates across the country, asking many of the same questions: What matters to voters now, what has changed and where is the country headed next?
So what will our hosts be listening for when Morning Edition hits the road? We asked them. Here are four things on their minds:
Steve Inskeep: "I am watching and listening for people who feel this election is personal. By which I mean that, beyond their general opinion of the state of the country, they feel they were directly affected by the events of the past two years — the Trump administration's dramatic moves to reshape immigration, government, education, science, research, the military, emergency management, taxes, foreign policy and the economy at large.
Michel Martin: "Ohio is also a key location for the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign, as well as a leading industrial and logistics hub, a place where we should be able to see how the administration's economic policies are playing out. Trump isn't on the ballot, but his policies are. So let's see how that's going.
"Michigan was once considered a big part of the Democrats' 'Blue Wall,' but in recent years has chosen both Democrats and Republicans in key races. And the Democratic base has had beef with the national party. So what's driving voters? Are they mad? Sad? Or just exhausted? We hope to find out."
Leila Fadel: "The path to controlling the Senate in part runs through Maine, and that's why we're reporting in the state before the midterm elections. I want to know what drives voters, and how much party loyalty still plays a role. Are their votes up for grabs? Or are they locked in along party lines?"
"This is a state that's seen some of the worst of the immigration crackdown; a man was killed by ICE. It has one of the longest borders with Canada, and so the trade war hits differently. The Democratic candidate Troy Jackson is facing incumbent Susan Collins, who has won her state five times before. So, we'll be asking what people want from their candidate and if it matters which party that resonating message comes from."
A Martínez: "Texas Republicans gerrymandered five congressional districts to favor the GOP in the upcoming midterms. In three of them, the new maps created more Latino voters."
"What's behind the Texas GOP's big bet on Latino voters, and will it help Republicans keep control of the U.S. Senate?"
Follow the reporting: Maine coverage airs today. Texas is up next on Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, and Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in the Up First newsletter.
Picture show
A new NPR series is taking readers and listeners to breakfast tables around the world. In Munich, Germany, a Bavarian breakfast typically consists of boiled veal sausage, sweet mustard and a giant pretzel, all washed down with beer. Demetrios Kyriakides, who spent a year researching Bavarian breakfast joints in Munich, says the ambiance of Gemütlichkeit, which describes conviviality, is just as important as the food. A meal is often accompanied by brass oom-pah-pah music. This feast is usually finished before the church bells ring at midday, signaling that all good things must come to an end. Check out these photos of breakfast in Munich.
3 things to know before you go
- Under artistic director Robert Garland, Dance Theatre of Harlem is embarking on a new era by reviving its landmark 1982 production of Firebird for an international tour.
- Biologists at the University of Massachusetts Amherst have found what may potentially be the world's loudest birds, and they all live in Brazil. (via WBUR)
- Scientist Olivia Sanderfoot wants to establish a new field called "smoke ecology," which studies the effects of wildfire smoke on wildlife and seeks ways to mitigate its impacts.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

npr.org.title: What voters in 6 key states could tell us about the 2026 midterms
npr.org.text:
What voters in 6 key states could tell us about the 2026 midterms
A version of this essay first appeared in the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get the news you need to start your day — plus a little fun — every weekday and Sunday.
Four weeks from now, the midterm elections will help decide the balance of power in Congress. And ahead of Election Day, Morning Edition will be traveling to six states with some of the most competitive races to hear what voters say is shaping their decisions.
We already have some clues about where voters stand. The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll found registered voters favor Democrats for Congress over Republicans by 12 percentage points. President Trump is also very much on voters' minds, with 45% saying their vote for Congress is a vote against him, compared with about a quarter who say they are voting to support him.
Across the political divide, one concern keeps rising to the top: the cost of living and what it means for people's economic futures.
But this year, some of the forces driving those costs are coming from far beyond voters' own communities. The war with Iran is affecting prices at the gas pump. Tariffs imposed in Washington are reaching the checkout counter. Foreign policy, economic policy and household costs are becoming harder to separate.
Republicans and Democrats are both campaigning on promises to make everyday life more affordable. But voters are weighing more than their bills. Immigration and the rapid growth of massive data centers are also part of the conversation. So is the voting process itself, including new restrictions that are raising questions about how ballots will be cast, secured and counted.
And in several of these states, another question hangs over the races: What do voters want from their own parties, and do old political loyalties still hold? Those are some of the questions that Morning Edition will take on the road, using the six states as a window into an electorate that is changing.
Steve Inskeep is reporting from North Carolina and Georgia, two closely watched Southern states. North Carolina has an open Senate seat and newly redrawn congressional districts. Georgia has competitive races for Senate and governor after several elections in which voters have backed candidates from both parties.
"I am watching and listening for people who feel this election is personal," Inskeep said.
He wants to hear from people who feel directly affected by the Trump administration's changes to immigration, government, education, taxes, foreign policy and the economy.
"Trump is not on the ballot but has urged voters to act as if he is, and given the consequential acts of his administration, voters are likely to respond as if he is," Inskeep said.
Michel Martin is headed to Ohio and Michigan, where some of the biggest questions are about political change in the Midwest. Ohio has competitive races for governor and Senate against a backdrop of economic anxiety. In Springfield, Martin will also look at how the end of temporary protected status for Haitians is affecting a community where Haitian immigrants make up a significant share of the population — and whether disagreements over immigration are changing how voters see their own parties.
Michigan offers a different set of tests. Trump won the state narrowly in 2024, when anger over the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza was a major issue for some voters, particularly in Michigan's Arab American communities. The state also saw a sharp increase in young-voter turnout. This year, an open Senate seat and a governor's race offer another chance to see whether those shifts are carrying into the midterms — and what role younger and Black voters are playing in the Democratic coalition.
Martin calls Ohio and Michigan "two big consequential states that have always told us a lot about where the rest of the country is, and is going."
In Michigan, she will be asking what is driving voters after the state has chosen both Democrats and Republicans in key races.
"Are they mad? Sad? Or just exhausted? We hope to find out," Martin said.
Leila Fadel is reporting from Maine, where a Senate race could help determine control of the chamber. Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking another term against Democrat Troy Jackson. Immigration and trade are also part of the political conversation there.
"I want to know what drives voters and how much party loyalty still plays a role," Fadel said. "Are their votes up for grabs? Or are they locked in along party lines?"
Maine's long border with Canada also gives the trade war a different dimension, as tariffs and tensions over cross-border trade affect businesses and communities with close economic ties to Canada. The state has also been affected by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. Fadel said she will be asking voters what they want from their candidates — and whether the party delivering that message matters.
A Martínez is heading to Texas, where Republicans are testing whether recent gains among Latino voters will hold. The state's U.S. Senate race has also put Texas in the national fight over control of the chamber.
Republicans redrew five congressional districts to favor the Republican Party in the midterms, including three with more Latino voters. Martínez said that this makes the party's strategy around Latino voters one of the questions he wants to examine.
"What's behind the Texas GOP's big bet on Latino voters, and will it help Republicans keep control of the U.S. Senate?"
Over the next four weeks, Morning Edition will report from races and electorates across the U.S., asking many of the same questions: What matters to voters now, what has changed and where is the country headed next?
Follow the reporting: Maine coverage airs today, Oct. 6. Texas is up next on Oct. 13, followed by reporting from North Carolina and Georgia and then Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition and NPR.org, as well as in the NPR app and the Up First newsletter.
This piece was edited by Treye Green.

npr.org.title: A history of presidents naming things after themselves (It's short. They rarely do)
npr.org.text:
A history of presidents naming things after themselves (It's short. They rarely do)
President Trump recently underscored his desire to have his name appear on the facade of the Kennedy Center with a threat. "Frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump told reporters. "It'll end up being ripped down."
Trump or his supporters have called for the president's name to appear on everything from naval battleships to airports. It's pretty rare for sitting presidents to stamp their identities on infrastructure, currency and other public assets — though history shows there are a few exceptions.
George Washington "didn't want a lot of fuss"
Discussions regarding this issue go all the way back to the first presidential administration.
"They were trying to figure out what was the right balance between the prestige required to give this new office respect, but also recognizing that they were not trying to re-create a monarchy," said Lindsay Chervinsky, executive director of the George Washington Presidential Library and author of The Cabinet: George Washington and the Creation of an American Institution.
Chervinsky said the issue first came up at the federal level during Washington's presidency around the Coinage Act of 1792. Congress was figuring out what to put on the inaugural American coins, given the habit in Great Britain and other nations of plastering the reigning monarch all over theirs.
"The House of Representatives said that the president should not be on currency because of this monarchical tie," Chervinsky said.
Chervinsky said Washington shared their concerns. The president usually shied away from ostentatious self-celebration. "He didn't want a lot of fuss," she said.
But sometimes, Washington didn't seem to mind it. "They did name the federal city Washington to honor him while he was still in office," Chervinsky said.
But what about the Hoover Dam?
Most administrations have generally kept the names and faces of sitting presidents off public assets since then, viewing it as unseemly.
On the few occasions when a sitting president's name has appeared — such as on dams named for Teddy Roosevelt, Calvin Coolidge and Woodrow Wilson — it tended not to be the man in office pushing for it himself. "Usually it is political supporters," Chervinsky said. And the history around the naming process can be fraught.
The most prominent example of this is the Hoover Dam.
The massive public works project located near the Boulder Canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border had been known in the early stages of its development as the Boulder Dam. Hoover's secretary of the interior, Ray Lyman Wilbur, suggested rechristening the project in 1930 as the Hoover Dam, owing to the lead role Hoover had played in its planning. "Hoover negotiated the deal among the states known as the Colorado River Compact that allocated the river's water among seven states," said Kenneth Whyte, author of Hoover: An Extraordinary Life in Extraordinary Times. "So it was generally agreed that it was deserved."
Apparently, the president thought so too. "Hoover, I think, was pleased about it," said Whyte. "But he did not talk a lot about it at the time. He didn't want to be seen to be doing self-aggrandizing things."
But the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration was having none of it. After Roosevelt took office in 1933, his secretary of the interior, Harold Ickes, called for the dam to revert to its original moniker.
"Ickes based this argument on the fact that the original legislation that authorized Congress to fund the project was called the Boulder Canyon Project Act," said Marist University's David Woolner, a senior fellow and resident historian at the Roosevelt Institute, and the author of several books about the 32nd U.S. president. "And he did not like the politics of Herbert Hoover."
Woolner said Roosevelt did not object to the change. He kept his political rival's name out of his 1935 dedication speech, consistently referring to it as "Boulder Dam."
The naming coup was short-lived.
Although there was some initial opposition from Democrats, in 1947, Congress voted unanimously to change the name back. Woolner said this happened "in recognition of Hoover's early support for the project, and after the former president gained praise for his humanitarian work during and after the First and Second World Wars."
There's always the presidential library ... or "library"
Roosevelt, for his part, wasn't "particularly anxious to have things named after him," Woolner said.
But that didn't stop Roosevelt from lending his name to one major project during his presidency — the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum — "which of course he initiated," said Woolner.
In keeping with this tradition, President Trump told reporters at a press briefing earlier this year he is planning to build himself a presidential library in Miami.
Except it probably won't be a library. And presidential libraries are, technically speaking, public-private assets.
"I don't believe in building libraries or museums," Trump said. "But it's most likely going to be a hotel with a beautiful building underneath and a 747 Air Force One in the lobby."
One thing that seems certain, judging by a video rendering on the president's social media channel promoting the project: Trump's name will be prominently displayed on its facade.

npr.org.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in physics for work on high-energy neutrinos from space
npr.org.text:
Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in physics for work on high-energy neutrinos from space
STOCKHOLM — Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in physics on Tuesday for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and his discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.
"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument. His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy," Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics, said in a news release.
Halzen spoke to the committee by phone from Italy on Tuesday.
"It was a great surprise and I obviously didn't expect it," he said.
Halzen said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize but the announcement still made him feel "strange."
Born in Belgium, the 82-year-old scientist is affiliated with the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the U.S. Efforts by The Associated Press to reach him were not immediately successful.
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory is a research facility located at the South Pole in Antarctica, according to its website, and the University of Wisconsin–Madison is its lead institution.
Neutrinos are tiny cosmic particles with a mind-bogglingly small mass. Yet they are everywhere: they spew from stars like the sun and trillions zip through our bodies every second.
Scientists can't glimpse the mysterious ghost particles zooming around on their own. Instead, they measure what happens when the tiny particles collide with other bits of matter, producing flashes of light or charged particles.
Halzen studied a rare gang of neutrinos that scientists consider messengers from the cosmos, offering clues to how the universe evolved.
His research into capturing neutrinos at the South Pole dates back to the 1980s.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the award in Stockholm.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.
Last year, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in physics for research on the strange behavior of subatomic particles called quantum tunneling that enabled the ultra-sensitive measurements achieved by MRI machines and laid the groundwork for better cellphones and faster computers.
The announcements of this year's prizes began Monday with the Nobel Prize in medicine being awarded to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works.
This week's awards continue Wednesday with the chemistry prize and literature on Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

npr.org.title: Disney, ABC battle Trump's FCC in court over free speech protections
npr.org.text:
Disney, ABC battle Trump's FCC in court over free speech protections
A federal court in Washington, D.C., is to play host to a legal battle Tuesday morning pitting the Walt Disney Co. against the nation's chief broadcast regulator over just how far First Amendment protections can go during the presidency of Donald Trump.
President Trump has repeatedly called for Disney's ABC TV to fire late night comedian Jimmy Kimmel, who has consistently mocked the president. Trump has also routinely denounced ABC's The View, accusing it of being liberal and unfair.
Trump had earlier sued the network, before returning to office, over incorrect statements anchor George Stephanopoulos made about the verdicts in writer E. Jean Carroll's two lawsuits against Trump. ABC paid $16 million in a December 2024 settlement, including legal fees, to resolve that a month before Trump went back to the White House. But new Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro has authorized a high-stakes fight against the administration in court.
Brendan Carr, whom Trump elevated to be the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, has echoed the president's complaints. And under Carr, the FCC is moving to review Disney's ownership of all eight of the stations it owns, as part of the ABC Network, years ahead of schedule. That followed months of social media posts from Trump urging that the FCC strip ABC of its station licenses.
"There's not even a question as to what Carr is doing. What Carr is doing is unconstitutional," says Mark Fowler, a Republican former FCC chair under President Ronald Reagan. Fowler has filed a statement to aid ABC's lawsuit in which he likened Carr's actions to censorship. "The First Amendment is very plain in its wording and its meaning," he says.
Technically, networks do not require licenses from the federal government to operate. Stations do need them to utilize publicly owned airwaves. They are perennially reviewed on a staggered basis and are typically renewed without much fanfare.
Carr has cited the requirement of stations to serve the "public interest," initiated investigations of Disney's diversity, equity and inclusion policies, and, though he says the license review is not linked to ABC's content, he has blasted the network as biased.
Disney and ABC are seeking to get U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan to issue an order preventing the FCC from accelerating the typical review process. She had compelled the FCC to hold off from moving ahead until this hearing. Media advocates, FCC veterans and legal observers say the move to challenge all ABC's local licenses at once is unprecedented. And were it to be successful, it would hurt ABC badly in the bottom line. Six of those eight stations are in major media markets and contribute significantly to the network's bottom line.
"The overreaching by the FCC is one of the greatest threats right now that's facing journalism," says Bruce Brown, the president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.
In an interview with NPR in August, Carr said that the agency has not decided whether to pull the station licenses from ABC. Instead, he said, ABC is complaining about his drive to take the "public interest" component of the law seriously. And he said that the network is getting ahead of itself. The agency has not yet taken any action against ABC's licenses — merely sped up their review.
That question may consume part of the legal wrangling on Tuesday as it will help determine whether ABC and Disney have standing to sue.
Conservative groups, including the fundraising outfits for U.S. Senate and House Republican candidates, filed briefs to support the FCC, and by extension, the president's complaints about bias.
"By any commonsense standard, evidence of broadcaster intent to advance the candidacies of Democratic Party figures on The View is not merely present, but overwhelming," the Republican fundraising committees say in a court filing.
Even so, several groups often affiliated with conservatives have weighed in against the Justice Department's case, including the Cato Institute, the Competitive Enterprise Institute and the Institute for Policy Innovation.
They note that Carr has roundly condemned ABC over its content, and in seeming direct echoes of Trump's condemnations — at one point saying on a right-wing podcast in September 2025 that ABC getting rid of Kimmel "can do this the easy way or the hard way." ABC suspended Kimmel hours later over remarks he made about the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.
The suspension was soon lifted after a public outcry.
Fellow satirists Seth Meyers of NBC's Late Night and John Oliver of HBO's Last Week Tonight paid tribute to their ABC counterpart during an episode of Jimmy Kimmel Live taped last week in Brooklyn.
"You come up all the time. [Fans] will normally say, how does it feel, being disliked by the current president? And we always say, as long as you're on the air, we're fine," Oliver told Kimmel. "We are fully behind you — the way we're fully behind a bulletproof vest."
The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press has filed a friend of the court brief on ABC's behalf, hiring a former U.S. solicitor general who has argued repeatedly before the U.S. Supreme Court, to represent the organization at the district court level.
Bruce Brown, president of the group, pointed at a series of other actions by Carr and other Trump appointees: The FCC has launched investigations into all broadcast networks, including NPR (save Fox, which is controlled by the president's allies, Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch); The administration has cut off access for many journalists at the White House and the Pentagon, while federal agents sought access to journalists' devices to identify anonymous sources; all the while, the president has sought to delegitimize media outlets whose presentation of the news has sparked public displays of anger.
"This is only one part of a wide effort by the Trump administration to intimidate the press — and to try to coerce out of news organizations the type of coverage the president wants to see," Brown says.

npr.org.title: Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey's new Pentagon roles raise ethics worries
npr.org.text:
Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey's new Pentagon roles raise ethics worries
A new Pentagon study focusing on the future of warfare is raising ethical concerns about its authors' potential conflicts of interest.
Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced "Project Meridian: The Future of Warfare," a study of automated and AI-powered weaponry.
In addition to former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, the other two leaders of the project are SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey, the co-founder of defense technology firm Anduril. The study is expected to take 120 days.
"We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare," Hegseth's September 30 announcement said. "To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them."
The study's announcement came just days before an expected speech by President Trump at an Anduril facility in Baltimore on Tuesday.
Anduril Industries builds military drones that are used on land, sea and in the air and other related defense technologies. The company received its initial funding from tech billionaire and conservative political activist Peter Thiel.
SpaceX has secured over $8 billion in U.S. defense contracts in 2026 alone, according to government contract announcements. One of its flagship products is Starshield, a military-grade, low-Earth-orbit satellite network designed to provide secure communications for the government. The company's AI chatbot, Grok, is also being used by the Pentagon.
There is a concern that Musk and Luckey's study would be guided by their own financial interests, said Richard Painter, a professor of corporate law at the University of Minnesota and former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.
"They all want to sell stuff," Painter said. "So if we go into it understanding that [Musk], like all the other contractors, he wants to make a lot of money selling AI to the Defense Department. Whatever he proposes, but it's not like he's doing it as a neutral public service."
"It's a massive conflict of interest," said a former senior Defense Department official who requested anonymity out of fear of reprisal from the Trump administration. The official said that not only do both Luckey and Musk have billions of dollars in current defense contracts, but the study could also shape the types of munitions the U.S. buys in the future. For example, it could recommend more drones or space-based assets — which both Luckey and Musk build — and fewer tanks, which they don't build.
Hegseth said he has directed Emil Michael, the Defense Department's chief technology officer, to commission Project Meridian through the MITRE Corporation, a nonprofit company that manages federally-funded research across the country. Few details were released about the scope of the project in Hegseth's one-page memo.
"MITRE is responsible for the analysis and recommendations, and will evaluate all inputs with technical rigor while applying appropriate conflict-of-interest and information safeguards," said a spokesperson for the Department of Defense. "The Project Meridian effort will examine the technologies and operational concepts required to sustain U.S. military advantage across the full spectrum of future warfighting domains across a 10-20 year time horizon."
The Department of Defense did not disclose whether Musk and Luckey have been hired as special government employees — as Musk was when he led the Department of Government Efficiency cost-cutting effort — or as contractors. The nature of their employment on the project would dictate the rules they would need to follow, Painter said.
Executive branch employees are bound by federal criminal law that bans them from taking part in government decisions that affect their own money or the financial interests of their family and business. Contractors, however, are not subject to this law.
The Department of Defense did not respond to questions about the potential conflicts of interests of hiring Musk and Luckey to lead the Project Meridian study. SpaceXAI and Anduril did not respond to requests for comment about their CEOs' potential conflicts of interest.
While it is common for the federal government to assemble task forces with industry leaders, the findings and recommendations of the Project Meridian study will need to be scrutinized, said a senior official at the Government Accountability Office, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press on issues they have not published reports on.
"There are safeguards that they're supposed to sign to keep them away from procurement activities and whatnot," the GAO official said. "That doesn't mean that we shouldn't be paying attention to what the project comes out with."
Additionally, the motivations for creating this task force are unclear, the official said.
"I don't know why we would need a new task force to talk about something since we've had many folks thinking about this issue for a while," the official said. "What would the point of this be?"
Another former Pentagon official who requested anonymity fearing retribution from the administration was less concerned. The official said there are always numerous efforts underway in the Pentagon and in the military services to ponder the future of war, and all those will likely feed into Project Meridian. The former official said it's one thing to be on such a panel and make recommendations, and for Congress to accept or reject them, and another for a panel member to write a requirement for a defense system and then bid on it.
The second Trump administration has employed different ethical standards than the administrations that preceded it, including holding stocks in companies that could stand to profit from contracts awarded by the government, Painter said.
"I do not know why they held on to defense stocks. In the Bush administration, we made everybody sell their defense stocks who went into the Defense Department," Painter said. "I never saw anywhere near as many financial conflicts of interest in any other administration. Even the first Trump administration wasn't as bad as this."

npr.org.title: Democrats' advantage is clear with less than a month to go in the midterm elections
npr.org.text:
Democrats' advantage is clear with less than a month to go in the midterm elections
President Trump was elected in 2024, in large measure, with a mandate to bring down prices. But that hasn't happened. Instead, Trump is facing record-low approval ratings, and voters are blaming him for costs that have continued to rise since he took office this second time around.
As a result, Republicans are likely to pay the price at the ballot box next month. One month out from Election Day, the electoral landscape has shifted even more so in Democrats' direction.
They are favored to win the House, albeit with a fairly narrow majority. The Cook Political Report forecasts a five-to-15-seat net gain for Democrats at this point. That would give them in the range of 220 to 230 seats come January. (218 is needed for a majority.)
The Senate has shifted more dramatically over the last several months. Six seats have moved more in Democrats' direction since June in comparing Cook's ratings from then to now. When the cycle first started, the Senate was a long shot for Democrats. Now, it's within reach.
And that's largely because of the national mood, which is usually the case in midterms. Trump has just a 37% approval rating, according to an average of the polls. That's tied for the lowest pre-midterm approval in the last half century.
The only other president to be that low in that time was George W. Bush in 2006. Back then, Iraq was spiraling into civil war, and Republicans lost both the House and Senate.
Trump is also facing a historic intensity of opposition; 53% in the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll said they strongly disapprove of the job the president is doing, the highest ever recorded in the survey. That's not a great sign for Republicans with Trump insisting that the midterm elections be about him.
As it is, history is unkind to the president's party in midterm elections. They usually lose about two dozen seats in the House and four in the Senate. It's even worse for the party in power when the president's approval rating is below 50%, as Trump's is now.
Loading...
There are multiple reasons Democratic gains might be limited, including mid-decade redistricting helping to insulate Republicans, fewer competitive-to-potentially competitive House seats, with most in districts Trump won in 2024, Republicans' campaign spending edge and the unpopularity of the Democratic Party.
That said, the headwinds the GOP is facing are very real.
Republicans have lost their edge on the economy
Economic issues continue to rate as the top problem and most important issue facing the country.
Most presidents get more blame and credit than they deserve for the economy, but the war with Iran and Trump's tariffs were choices that have directly led to increased costs on many goods and energy.
The economy is increasingly bifurcated with the wealthy doing well and regular people struggling. Wealthy Americans are seeing increases in their wealth and stock portfolios, which are dominated by AI companies.
It's a different story for many others. Inflation is outpacing wages, meaning people's paychecks aren't taking them as far. There isn't a lot of turnover in the labor market, so if someone doesn't have a job or is looking to change, it's not an easy thing to do.
Plus, many are turning against AI. In many places, it's driving up utility costs and, along with the rising national debt, is making borrowing more difficult.
All of that is coming at a time when gas prices have skyrocketed because of the Iran war, and interest rates are creeping higher. In trying to tame inflation, the Federal Reserve hiked rates this fall. That makes it more expensive to borrow money and harder to pay for things like houses and cars.
The blame for that sort of thing often gets pointed directly at the White House and the party in power, and right now, that's Trump and Republicans.
An AP/NORC poll released last week, for example, found that 65% said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump's policies than factors outside of his control.
Just 26% said they approved of the job he's doing on the economy.
An NBC News poll from September found that for only the second time in the Trump era, respondents said they trusted Democrats more than Republicans on the economy. (Though it was within the margin of error, the movement in the survey was clear.)
The only other time Democrats led on that question was in 2018 – the last midterm year when Trump was president. Democrats won 42 seats and control of the House then.
Add the widely negative views of the economy to the administration's immigration enforcement tactics, discretionary domestic cuts, the slashing of regulations and the government workforce, and it's all firing up Democrats.
An opposition party enthusiastic to vote is a major warning sign for the president's party, especially in a midterm year.
History is not on the side of the president's party in midterm elections
In 18 of the 20 midterms since World War II, the president's party has lost House seats. On average, it's 26 seats, and it's nine more than that when a president's approval rating is below 50%.
The last three midterm elections have seen fewer lost House seats, despite unpopular presidents, in large measure because the universe of competitive districts is smaller.
The president, himself, though, has acknowledged multiple times the political headwinds his party faces in midterms.
"Whether you have a great president or not, Republican or Democrat, they don't do well in midterms," Trump said Friday at a campaign rally in Alabama. "I don't know why. Nobody's explained it."
There are reasons, however.
First, turnout in midterms is historically about 30% lower than in presidential years. So, the voters most fired up to vote show up in outsized numbers.
Anger is a great motivator, and often the voters more aligned with the opposition party most want to register their frustration. And, as noted earlier, the intensity of opposition to Trump is at historic levels.
A CBS poll out Sunday found Democrats with the enthusiasm edge – 84% of Democrats and 82% of independents surveyed said they are "definitely" going to vote compared to 77% of Republicans.
What's more, a key indicator of which party does well in midterms is pointing in the Democrats' direction. Surveys, including the NPR/PBS News/Marist poll, ask a version of: "If November's election for Congress were held today, which party's candidate are you more likely to vote for in your district?"
In an average of the 2026 polls, Democrats have a nine-point advantage on this question, known as the congressional ballot test. Democrats tend to need a larger lead on the question historically than Republicans, given how districts have been drawn. But +9 is in the range of what Democrats need.
To put a finer point on it: in each of the past seven midterm elections, the party with the advantage on the congressional ballot has made gains.
Loading...
With independents and Latinos, two swing groups, souring on Trump during this second term, that's an added problem for Republicans in competitive districts.
Their jobs are made even tougher when Trump says things like "pretend" he's on the ballot and makes the election a "referendum" on him.
The White House's theory of the case is that Trump has had success turning conservatives out when he's on the ballot, and Republican candidates need them to show up in big numbers.
But whether that's enough is going to be tested. In swing districts and some key Senate races, candidates also usually need voters in the middle to win.
The bottom line is with less than a month to go until all the votes are in, the political compass is pointed in Democrats' direction. For multiple reasons, Democrats' gains might not be as big as similar numbers might indicate in past elections, but there is no doubt that, right now, they have the wind at their backs.

theguardian.com.title: Shadow minister says Tories would ‘keep political activism out of classrooms’ – UK politics live
theguardian.com.text:
Laura Trott says Tories would 'keep political activism out of classroom' - in speech to near-empty hall
Laura Trott, the education secretary, has given a speech at the conference. This morning the events are on the main stage, which is the smaller venue. This afternoon events are in the larger symphony hall.
Trott’s speech was largely a long rant about supposed political correctness excesses in schools, with pupils being told that white people are privileged, women can have penises, Britain is racist etc. She said the Tories would “keep political activism out of the classroom”.
Trott is now taking part in a panel discussion including the Telegraph journalist and GB News presenter Camilla Tominey. Tominey is no leftie, but even she seemed to think Trott had laid it on a bit too thick. Tominey said that, following the supreme court judgment, she thought children were no longer being told women can have penises.
There aren’t many people watching – either in the hall or on YouTube, where there is a live feed.
But the Labour press office is tuning in. It has just posted this picture of the event on social media with the heading “People disguised as chairs latest” – a reference to a joke told by Jeremy Clarkson yesterday, when he was sarcastically commenting on how good it was to see so many people in the audience for his Tory conference session.
Shadow education secretary says Tories would legislate to stop teaching unions bringing politics into classroom
Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, may have been speaking to a minuscule audience in the hall earlier (see 11.18am), but she gave a long speech that covered quite a lot of ground. Here are the main points.
Trott said the Tories would legislate to stop teaching unions bringing politics into the classroom. She spoke at length about pupils being exposed to unsuitable political content in the classroom and she said:
Today I’m launching Our Pledge to Parents which lays out my commitment to mums and dads. I will keep political activism out of the classroom.
And she singled out teaching unions for particular criticism.
We’ll properly enforce the rules on political impartiality for teachers and guest speakers.
And we’ll create a specific law around trade unions involved in education.
They must not bring politics into schools.
She claimed that pupils were being exposed to unsuitable ideas in the classroom.
Children as young as seven are being told they have white privilege.
Pupils are learning that a woman can have a penis, a man can be pregnant, and sex is assigned at birth.
Some have been told to rewrite negative headlines on migration to make them more positive.
And others have been taught that Britain is a racist country.
This is fiction being presented as fact ….
This is part of a trend of complex, controversial, contested issues being boiled down, laced with political bias and delivered in a place that children trust; schools.
If anyone has an agenda, it’s a network called Schools of Sanctuary.
Now you might not have heard of it, but it has now signed up over a thousand sixth forms, secondary schools, primary schools, even nurseries,
All calling themselves schools of sanctuaries for refugees.
The vision schools are signing up to is that the UK will be a place of welcome for all.
Except it’s more nuanced than that isn’t it?
We can’t welcome all migrants.
We don’t want to welcome all migrants, certainly not dangerous criminals.
Yet that is the simplistic political narrative they push on our children.
But when I wrote to the former education secretary [Bridget Phillipson] about this blatant political activism, do you know what she did?
Absolutely nothing.
She also condemned the role played by the National Education Union, England’s largest teaching union, in schools.
What do you think they debate when the NEU, that’s the National Education Union, get together?
The merits of teaching Latin perhaps?
The value of coding in maths?
The latest developments in pedagogy?
No.
Their recent resolutions include:
Defending the right to protest, opposing UK defence spending and embedding their own LGBT+ teaching materials in schools.
Friends, this doesn’t sound like a professional body that cares about teaching pupils.
It sounds like a campaigning organisation bent on politicising education.
And it is deeply entwined with politics, extreme politics.
Several NEU officials happen to also be directors of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign.
She said there was too much antisemitism in schools.
Parents … are being left with an impossible choice.
Sending their children to mainstream schools where Jewish children are heckled, bullied, singled out, or send them to Jewish schools, with prison-like securitywhere they’re under constant threat from outside.
She said under the Tories state schools would not be allowed to force young girls to wear the hijab. Referring to this story, she said:
You might have heard about the school in Barnet making the hijab part of the uniform for girls as young as 7.
Conference, be absolutely clear, we would not allow that under a future Conservative government.
She said the Tories and Labour had fundamentally different approaches to education.
Lucy Powell [the education secretary] says, education should be about what you can do, and not what you can’t.
Cartlidge says 'Iron Dome' just generic term for missile defence, like 'Hoover' meaning vacuum cleaner
James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, has suggested that, when the Tories talked about setting up an “Iron Dome”, they were just using it as a generic term for missile defence – like describing a vacuum cleaner as a Hoover. They were not talking about the Israeli version, he claimed.
In an attempt to clear up the confusion caused by the Tories first saying they were proposing an Israeli-type Iron Dome, before Kemi Badenoch later said that wasn’t the plan (see 7.59am), Cartlidge told the Press Association:
The phrase ‘iron dome’ has come to be used a bit like the word ‘Hoover’ to generically refer to missile defence systems – and this is clearly a missile defence system.
Is it the exact same iron dome as Israel? No.
The Israeli iron dome is a short-range system. It’s to do with very near threats from the likes of Hezbollah.
It was actually originally designed for artillery and very unsophisticated weaponry, whereas what we’re talking about, Britannia Shield, is a bespoke UK system.
It’s just, if you speak to the media and the public, if you say ‘iron dome’, they at least know roughly what you’re talking about.
Katie Lam, the shadow communities secretary, also spoke this morning to a near-empty hall. She said she was launching a programme to develop “a new Conservative vision for local government”.
Explaining what that meant, she said:
That vision has to be informed by the wealth of experience that we have in our party.
Whether that’s councillors, former councillors, or just people who know about their area, and who have ideas about how it should be run.
It is widely assumed that, under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, moderate, one-nation Conservatives have been more or less wiped out as a force in the party. But, in her Guardian column based on her time at the conference, Polly Toynbee suggests they might be more resilient than we think.
Here is an extract.
If nothing improves by next conference, the mirage of Badenoch’s rock-solid support will melt away. But what would replace her? Waiting in the wings there is a model of what a Conservative revival might look like – Prosper UK, launched in January.
It tiptoes, praising Badenoch loudly, yet it is running seven events at this conference. That included a small Sunday night rally for electoral reform. It was addressed by former West Midlands mayor Andy Street, now co-chair of Prosper UK with Ruth Davidson It is backed by a formidable array of what was once the One Nation group, now defunct in parliament – or dormant under Badenoch’s rightwards march. No MPs back Prosper UK in public, but the group claims a third of them do secretly, along with 30,000 declared supporters. David Gauke, vice chair, has crept back into the party – he thinks by accident when the membership computer processing his re-application didn’t register he’d been ejected in 2019. In returning, he joined a battalion of remainer luminaries of the centre-right who’d had the whip suspended at the same time, including Kenneth Clarke and Dominic Grieve.
Gauke travels the country speaking to Conservative associations and others. Prosper UK is pro-EU, pro-migration for skilled workers and foreign students, pro-net zero and against the pension triple lock – and Gauke says that “Conservatives should be truth tellers on all these”. But though socially liberal, he’s dry as a bone on fiscal discipline, campaigning for low business taxes, a smaller state and enticing back non-doms – all Hayek, no Keynes. “No one speaks for some 7 million people centre or centre-right,” he says.
Badenoch suggests Tories would not reverse Labour legislation making pensions triple lock less generous
In her interview with Times Radio this morning, Kemi Badenoch hinted that, if Labour has legislated to make the pensions triple lock less generous by the time of the next election, a future Tory government would not reverse that.
In his party conference speech last week, Andy Burnham said he wanted to change the triple lock uprating mechanism from 2030, with the savings used to part fund his plans to set up a National Care Service. The government later said it would legislate for this before the election.
The Tories are committed to the pensions triple lock in its current form. But, asked if she would repeal any legislation passed making it less generous, Badenoch replied:
I have said that the triple lock is our policy and it remains our policy. I don’t think going after pensioners is the right thing when there are loads of people who can work, who won’t work.
When we are going to reverse Labour’s policies, I say we are going to reverse their policies.
I have said that we are keeping this policy, but if they take that money and they spend it on something that we can’t get it back from, then it would be difficult for me.
What I’m not going to do is lie to your listeners just so I can get votes. I tell the truth and I say the triple lock is our policy and we’re keeping it.
But what I’m not going to do is to say something when I don’t know what the situation would be about what Labour has done with that money. We have to be very careful.
Laura Trott says Tories would 'keep political activism out of classroom' - in speech to near-empty hall
Laura Trott, the education secretary, has given a speech at the conference. This morning the events are on the main stage, which is the smaller venue. This afternoon events are in the larger symphony hall.
Trott’s speech was largely a long rant about supposed political correctness excesses in schools, with pupils being told that white people are privileged, women can have penises, Britain is racist etc. She said the Tories would “keep political activism out of the classroom”.
Trott is now taking part in a panel discussion including the Telegraph journalist and GB News presenter Camilla Tominey. Tominey is no leftie, but even she seemed to think Trott had laid it on a bit too thick. Tominey said that, following the supreme court judgment, she thought children were no longer being told women can have penises.
There aren’t many people watching – either in the hall or on YouTube, where there is a live feed.
But the Labour press office is tuning in. It has just posted this picture of the event on social media with the heading “People disguised as chairs latest” – a reference to a joke told by Jeremy Clarkson yesterday, when he was sarcastically commenting on how good it was to see so many people in the audience for his Tory conference session.
Air Marshal Greg Bagwell, former deputy commander of RAF Air Command, told Times Radio he did not think the Tories pledge of £10bn over 10 years would be enough to fund a missile defence system that would protect the UK, its territories and bases.
As the Press Association reports, Bagwell said:
It really is a question of definition of what capability you’re going to deliver here, and what you can realistically expect in terms of protection.
You might be able to protect certain key sites, certain strategic areas. London would be an example, but of course that’s not enough.
If you’ve got military bases all around the country, you’ve got power stations, you’ve got critical infrastructure dotted around the country, then you’re really going to have to try and cover the entire area, which is is challenging.
Bagwell said a full system could cost more than £80bn. He said that the US was talking about spending between $200bn and $1tr (£150bn to £750bn) for their “Golden Dome”.
Bagwell’s analysis matches what General Sir Richard Barrons told MPs in the summer. (See 10.23am.)
According to the BBC, Sidharth Kaushal, a senior fellow at the defence thinktank RUSI, said that while £10bn would not fund an Israeli-style “Iron Dome” missile defence system, it would “probably cover” what the UK “actually needs” including horizon radar and more E7 aircrafts.
How Tories would fund their £1bn-a-year 'Britannia Shield' plan
According to the Conservatives, a Tory government would fund the plan for a £1bn-a-year “Britannia Shield” with some of the money from the extra £10bn a year it would raise for defence.
Last month, the Tories published details of how that £10bn a year would be funded. Some £8bn of that would come from cuts to benefits – £4bn from cutting housing benefit, £3bn from reimposing the two-child benefit cap, and £1bn from the Motability scheme funding cars for disabled people.
The housing benefit cuts would partly be achieved by cutting local housing allowance (LHA) rates, which determine how much people can receive in housing benefit. The Tories have briefed that LHA rates would be set at 10th percentile of local market rates, not the 30th percentile.
The cuts would also involve social sector rents being cut.
How General Sir Richard Barrons told MPs ideal missile defence system would cost £120bn
Kemi Badenoch was asked earlier (see 7.59am) about GeneralSir Richard Barrons, the retired former head of Joint Forces Command, saying an Iron Dome-style missile defence system would cost up to £100bn.
The subject of integrated air and missile defence also links to the absolutely vital point that gets lost so often: the defence investment plan is the articulation of the SDR [strategic defence review] – it is the things that made the cut for the money available. Given the legacy holes in defence, there is at least another half of the iceberg that never made it into the DIP, because it was not even remotely affordable. There is a £60 billion to £80 billion hole in defence infrastructure—falling down airfields, ports, housing, the Reserve Forces’ and Cadets’ Associations. Most of that is not in the DIP, because it just could not get into the cut.
Integrated air and missile defence is the iconic thing that did not make into the review. There is about £1 billion in the DIP for it, and that buys improved command and control – you’ll know better that you’re going to be hit by a missile – some improvements for the Air Force ability to shoot down cruise missiles, and some improvements to the Type 45 so that it has a better capability against ballistic missiles.
Many people in the country assume there is a sort of iron dome over at least London, and that is not even remotely there. Even if you embrace the extraordinary technological change that some companies are producing in low-cost kills, whether directed energy weapons, DragonFire or cheaper missiles like Cambridge Aerospace and that kind of thing, the cost of an iron dome at entry level is probably £80 billion over 10 years—entry level. The IAMD [integrated air and missile defence] of my dreams is probably £120 billion over 10 years. But we got £1 billion, because it sits in that bit of the iceberg that never got to be remotely affordable. We should not kid ourselves that if we have an argument about the margins of the DIP, we are somehow fixing defence. That is just not true.
Here is Jessica Elgot’s story about the Tory “Iron Dome” spin gaffe.
As Jess points out, the Conservatives did not just call their plan an Iron Dome in their press release; Kemi Badenoch used the phrase too, in an article published under her name in the Sun.
Badenoch disowns her own party's claim that proposed missile defence plan amounts to 'British Iron Dome'
Kemi Badenoch is now on GB News.
Talking about the Tory plans for a “Britannia Shield”, she says:
It is not an Iron Dome like what Israel has. It is not something used to cover the entire country.
This is her final interview from the morning round, and it ends with Badenoch, even more firmly then before, quashing the line that the Conservatives were using in a news release (see 7.59am) sent out less than 24 hours ago.

In her interview on Times Radio earlier, Kemi Badenoch said she had been reading about how some “heritage brands” recovered after losing their reputation for tips that might help the Tories.
She said:
I’ve been reading a lot about heritage brands that lost their way. And it always happens when the brand stops looking after its core customers and starts doing things that are off-brand. And it takes some time to recover from that.
But that is what I’m doing. Refreshing the brand. I’m glad that I’m doing well. I know that people have started listening to the Conservative party again. I want them to start buying.
Badenoch says she does not understand why people are policing others’ identity.
I don’t understand why all of a sudden some people are policing other people’s identity?
I think identity is something very personal. If that’s how [Braverman] feels about herself, I think that’s fine.
