I think we need we need to be very careful with this, sort of conversation.
She says, on gender, she thinks men are men and women are different.
But identity is different. Her children are half white, half black.
Q: But isn’t Braverman saying that black footballers playing for England are not English?
Badenoch says Braverman must speak for herself. She says she personally would not say those footballers are not English.
Q: Do you think Kemi Badenoch would be welcome as a migrant to the UK today?
Badenoch says when she was born in England in 1980 thinks were very different. Two years later the rules were changed. (Badenoch gave British citizenship because she was born in the country, but that rule changed.”

theguardian.com.title: Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying
theguardian.com.text:
A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has been arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency, prosecutors said.
August Hanning, 80, was head of the federal intelligence service (BND) – which operates outside Germany to gather information across the fields of political, economic, and military intelligence – between 1998 and 2005.
He was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster early on Tuesday. His former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, was arrested at the same time in Bavaria, on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”, according to a prosecutor’s statement. Media pictures showed Hanning, dressed in an open-necked white shirt, being taken from his redbrick house to a bullet-proof vehicle by masked officers.
Manfred D, who continued to work for Hanning’s successors at the BND after Hanning’s departure until the present day, is accused of using his role to gain access to classified information which he then handed to Hanning “in exchange for payment”, the prosecutors’ statement continued.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
Prosecutors believe that Hanning intended to resell the documents as part of a paid consulting role he had built up after leaving the BND, prosecutors added. To what extent and to whom he disseminated them remains part of an ongoing investigation.
He is accused of using the information to “draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service”, prosecutors said. It was unclear if this information had reached its intended recipient, they added.
Over several years Hanning is also believed to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, in part based on information passed to him by Manfred D, to a close contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.
Several properties connected to both men were being searched simultaneously on Tuesday, including in Berlin.
Manfred D is due to appear before judges at the federal court of justice in Karlsruhe later on Tuesday, while Hanning is scheduled to appear on Wednesday.
Suspicions over Hanning’s activities emerged as a result of an investigation into the kidnappings of the children from a prominent Hamburg business family, which is the focus of a major trial in the north German port city.
Investigators were led to Hanning over allegations, which he denies, that he helped Christina Block, the heiress of a steak restaurant dynasty, to organise the violent cross-border seizure in Denmark of her children from her estranged husband who has custody of two of their children. Block denies the charges.
After he left the BND, Hanning worked as a global consultant in the fields of security and business, based on his credentials as former intelligence chief. He is considered to have been well connected with government and business sectors in Russia and China.
Hanning was an officer stationed at the embassy-equivalent organisation for West Germany in communist East Berlin. After his role as president of the BND ended in 2005 he became the highest-ranking official in Germany’s security sector as the head of all security agencies under the federal interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble.

theguardian.com.title: Trump says he will stop using taxpayer funds for self-promoting ads after backlash – US politics live
theguardian.com.text:
Donald Trump has said he will stop using taxpayer funds for television advertisements glorifying himself, which sparked a major backlash, and instead tap his super PAC to cover ads going forward.
In a post on his social media site, Trump defended the ads, which cost at least $1.5m in federal funds and have drawn intense criticism. Trump said they were “positive promotion for our Great U.S.A”.
“This is a rather standard thing to do,” the president wrote, while blaming intense criticism for using taxpayer funds on the ads on the “Radical Left.”
But the president added that he had “decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
Trump provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such future advertising, AP reported.
The White House - which had fiercely defended using taxpayer money on spots meant to promote the president - said on Monday night that MAGA Inc will pay for such ads going forward. It did not answer questions on how it or Trump might prove that his political funds were being used on such future advertising.
The first ad featured clips of Trump talking about defeating communism interspersed with onscreen text promoting the “largest tax cuts in history,” “reigniting American manufacturing” and a call to “defend law and order and police.”
Later the same week, a second ad began running. It showed scenic videos of Mount Rushmore with quotes and clips from Trump’s 4th July weekend speech there honoring the country’s 250th anniversary.
In other developments:
Donald Trump said he was “doing great” as his approval rating sank to a record low 32%. The president made the remarks as he headed to Nebraska, to campaign for a Republican senator there.
Pennsylvania is reporting the largest measles outbreak in the nation, with more than 1,000 cases this year. The governor of neighboring New York, Kathy Hochul, has declared a disaster emergency over an ongoing measles outbreak there.
Politico was barred from traveling on Air Force One for Trump’s trip to Nebraska, according to a report by CNN. This comes after the administration previously stopped CNN from similarly traveling with the president, despite a federal judge putting a temporary block on Trump’s overall ban on Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House.
Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is joining Fox News as an on-air contributor, according to an announcement from the network. Leavitt, 29, the youngest press secretary in White House history, left the administration after the birth of her second child earlier this year.
The supreme court heard the first arguments of its 2026-27 term, in a case that focuses on whether states can sue oil companies for the impact of climate change on their communities. The lawsuit was filed by local officials in Boulder, Colorado, against Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil.
Secretary of state Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of US bombers from a UK airbase and a suspected Iranian plot at the site last week. “I wouldn’t just directly tie that to the move that was made,” Rubio told reporters, when asked about the B1 bombers. “The Department of War is constantly reallocating resources where they need to be,“ Rubio added, noting that the US has confidence in the security of all its bases.
Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington. At 1pm ET, he and first lady Melania Trump will welcome Gold Star families to the White House for a reception. We’ll then hear from the president at 4pm ET when he travels to Baltimore County, Maryland, where’s he due to deliver remarks at Tradepoint Atlantic, an industrial center. According to the Baltimore Banner – a local outlet – Anduril Industries, a defense technology manufacturer is expected to make an announcement about the company’s future at the facility.
A reminder that Anduril Industries is owned by Palmer Luckey, a top Trump donor. The Guardian has previously reported that Luckey’s company has received billions in contracts from the administration for drones, autonomous jet fighters and space-based interceptors.
Last week, Pete Hegseth also announced that Luckey, Elon Muskand Newt Gingrich will co-lead a government project to study the “future of warfare”.
In Donald Trump’s telling, he’s a model of incorruptible self-sacrifice.
“I’m the only president that donated his salary,” he told a group of cheering supporters at a Hispanic heritage month celebration in the White House last week, before conceding that George Washington – “a very wealthy person” – might have beaten him to the punch.
“They pay me $550,000 a year, and in my first term, I donated it,” he continued. “In my second term I donated it too. I donated it to fixing the White House. I donated the salary into the White House preservation.”
Trump’s ethical self-depiction was undercut in startling fashion a day later when the crypto company that runs his memecoin offered “the most exclusive dinner in the world” at the president’s members-only Trump National club in Washington.
“Join three legends and featured speaker Donald J Trump,” gushed the invite to the 185 biggest investors in the Trump coin. The top 29 buyers were promised an invitation to an additional “VIP reception with your favourite president and one of the legends”. For the top four donors, a Trump 18-karat gold watch lay in store.
The aim appeared to be to boost sales of the memecoin – called $Trump – over the next two months. Trump personally profits from the coin, and disclosures show he made about $636m from it last year.
With just over a month to go before November’s midterm elections, Democrats seized on the dinner invitation as a political gift as they try to convert concerns over Trump’s perceived corruption into a groundswell of outrage. They theorize it will power a “blue wave” that could enable the party to retake control of the House of Representatives and the Senate on 3 November.
Trump suggests he would let Iran ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
Lauren Gambino
Leaders in California have denounced Donald Trump as “reckless” and “deranged” after the US president suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego – two liberal cities in the blue state that has been a frequent target of his administration.
At a rally in ruby red Nebraska on Monday night, Trump told supporters that he hoped to see a “tremendous victory” in the fast-approaching November midterm elections. He then suggested high prices due to the war with Iran were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”.
“They can take out a city,” Trump said in Grand Island. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded.
“It’ll be over very soon,” Trump said of the war.
The governor and the cities’ mayors quickly condemned the comments. “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said on X. “He is deranged and dangerous.”
Newsom, a Democrat who has repeatedly clashed with Trump over his two terms, said from his press office account: “Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America’s largest cities. This is not normal. None of this is. And we will continue to remind folks of that every day.”
Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, assailed the president for making what she called “irresponsible threats” that “could potentially compromise” the safety of America’s second-largest city.
“The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” she said in a statement.
New Jersey congresswoman LaMonica McIver faces legal deadline after giving birth to second child
Rachel Leingang
A US congresswoman who just gave birth to a baby girl faces a deadline this week on whether to seek a rehearing of a federal case against her by the Trump administration after an oversight visit to an immigration detention facility.
LaMonica McIver, 40, represents New Jersey’s 10th congressional district. She gave birth to her second child last Thursday – a rarity for a sitting member of Congress. She is only the 15th member of Congress to give birth while serving and part of a small subset of congresswomen who have school-age children.
McIver first won her seat during a special election in mid-2024, then won a full term later that year. She is also running for re-election this year.
In announcing the birth of her second child after publicly discussing fertility struggles, McIver called being a mom “one of the greatest joys of my life”.
“Getting the chance to raise a family is a priority and a delight for me, something I hope everyone who wants to, gets the chance to do,” she said in a statement last week. “Bringing a child into the world is a reminder not only of why we fight for maternal healthcare and reproductive rights, but of why we fight for the rights and freedoms of our most vulnerable – they are someone’s babies too.”
In late August, a federal appeals court declined to dismiss criminal charges against McIver, who is charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility that has drawn protests over poor conditions inside. She is the only member of Congress whom the Department of Justice has indicted, and the charges carry a potential 17 years in prison.
She has pleaded not guilty to the charges and sought to get them dismissed, arguing that she is immune from prosecution under the US constitution’s speech and debate clause because she was doing her job and that she has been selectively prosecuted by the Trump administration.
Some Republicans also raised concerns, with Senate majority leader, John Thune, and the senators Mike Rounds, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis questioning the use of public money.

theguardian.com.title: Argentina to stop Falklands exploiting offshore oilfields, country’s foreign minister says
theguardian.com.text:
Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that his government would stop the Falkland Islands from exploiting its offshore oilfields as part of a strategy to take sovereignty.
During a speech at a thinktank event in the Argentinian capital, Pablo Quirno condemned the British government for failing to open negotiations over the islands and facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters.
Among those in the audience was David Cairns, the UK’s ambassador to Argentina. Cairns, who was photographed listening to Quirno, left the event shortly after the foreign minister returned to his seat.
Quirno told the audience at the event organised by the Argentine Council for International Relations that his country’s president, Javier Milei, had a strategy for the “peaceful” assertion of Argentinian sovereignty.
He said: “The British government not only refuses to enter into negotiations to resolve the sovereignty dispute, but is also taking unilateral measures regarding the exploitation of natural resources in the maritime areas that are part of the controversy.
“Preventing the exploitation of our resources from consolidating the British occupation is part of a strategy to recover, through peaceful means, the full exercise of our sovereignty.”
Last month, Milei told the UN general assembly in New York that the international organisation had failed his country as he condemned the Sea Lion project, an oil development in the North Falkland Basin, as an “unlawful act”.
Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline stop the oil project or face arbitration and a binding decision under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS) at the international tribunal for the law of the sea.
The UN does not officially recognise British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
The 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.
The UK government has said that the islands, known as Las Malvinas in Argentina and which are home to approximately 3,600 people, will remain a British overseas territory for as long as it is the wish of those who live there. In a referendum in 2013, on a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
In a statement issued last week, the Argentinian govenment rejected “the manipulation of the principle of self-determination of peoples that the United Kingdom seeks to impose upon it”.
In his speech on Monday night, Quirno also warned third parties that they should not assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of the natural resources.
A new shipping link is due to be opened between Chile and the Falkland Islands by the end of the year.
Quirno said: “Whoever contributes, directly or indirectly, to the illegitimate exploration or exploitation of resources that belong to all Argentinians will hardly be able to aspire to share in the benefits of our country’s growth.”

theguardian.com.title: Australia faces summer of extreme weather, Anthony Albanese warns at pre-Cop
theguardian.com.text:
Anthony Albanese has warned Australia faces a hazardous summer, likely including floods, cyclones and extreme heat, due to the immediate threat of the climate change and a rising “super El Niño”.
Speaker alongside national leaders at a climate summit in Fiji, the prime minister said the expected nasty summer and the demonstrated impact on Pacific island countries – including low-lying Tuvalu – showed the world could not afford to let the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C “just slip from our grasp”.
“Climate change is not a problem for the future. It is here right now, and we know that sea levels here in the western Pacific are rising at more than twice the global average. We know also that the forecast of super El Niño may test us all,” he said
“In Australia, we are expecting a summer of floods, of cyclones, of extreme heat, and extreme behaviour…The science told us that if we didn’t act to address global emissions this is precisely what would occur, and tragically that is playing out.”
Albanese’s comments came after a delegation of national and global agency leaders visited Tuvalu to see the impact of the climate crisis on one of the countries most at risk. A collection of three reef islands and six atolls, Tuvalu is home to about 10,000 people and mostly less than 2 metres above sea level.
The visit was promised by the Albanese government last year as part of a compromise deal when it missed out on hosting the Cop31 climate conference. Cop31 will be in Turkey next month; Fiji and Tuvalu are hosting a preparatory meeting.
Tuvalu was wet and grey for the visit, and the capital of Funafuti – spectacular from the air on a clear day – was visible only in strips between heavy rain clouds during descent.
After a cultural welcome and a tour of a climate resilience project, leaders held a “sautalaga” meeting – an exchange of views – where they expressed support for the country and urged more rapid action to cut emissions and provide island states with the money needed to adapt.
The delegation heard from Melelusi Sokotia, a 13-year-old local student, who said her friends dreamed of “becoming teachers, doctors, builders” but spent their lives wondering if their island would survive into their adult lives. “We all have one single dream: to grow safely here in Tuvalu,” she said. “We are not asking for peace. We are asking for help and partnership. Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”
Tuvalu’s prime minister, Feleti Teo, stressed island states needed faster access to global climate finance to deal with worsening extreme events. “Why should countries like Tuvalu take on more debt to protect ourselves from a climate crisis we did so little to cause? We should not have to borrow our way out of a crisis.”
The Fijian prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said the world was on the brink of overshooting the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C – agreed in the 2015 Paris agreement – and must bring forward plans to cut emissions. “That is not radical. It is in line with our agreement, our obligation, and the scientific reality,” he said. “The transition away from fossil fuels was agreed to by all of us in Dubai [at the Cop28 summit in 2023]. It is not a new ask, and it is not open for renegotiation.”
Australia has faced criticism at the talks for arguing for greater climate action while continuing to new expanded coal and gas developments. An Australian state regulator last week approved a major coalmine development that would be the largest in New South Wales’ history if it receives federal approval.
Albanese, attending his first UN climate conference as prime minister since his election in 2022, said a message from the Tuvalu trip was that “climate change must be understood as being something more than about science or targets”. “It must be understood that effectively it’s about people,” he said.
The delegation, which include former Australian prime minister Julia Gillard, now the chair of health charity Wellcome, were shown a land reclamation project to extend the atoll by about 20 hectares using sand and gravel dredged from its lagoon.
Tuvalu’s director of climate change, Jamie Ovia, told the visitors sea level rise was projected to increase the annual cost of damage from flooding and storm surges to US$34m a year by 2050 and $63m – more than Tuvalu’s GDP – by 2100.
He said the coastal fishing catch could be reduced by 16% and tuna stocks worth $4m a year could be lost as seas warmed. “We need time to adapt,” Ovia said. “Tuvalu is doing our part. Will you act with Tuvalu and will you act in time?”

theguardian.com.title: Former UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in Gaza
theguardian.com.text:
A former senior UN food agency official has alleged he was fired last week for his work highlighting hunger in Gaza, and has launched an appeal against his dismissal.
Benjamin Davis said the leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) had refused to renew his contract as director of its rural transformation and gender equality division because his team had published a brief on hunger in Gaza and held a seminar on the subject last year, and because he taken part in weekly “moment of silence” vigils on FAO grounds for those killed.
The seminar on hunger in Gaza last September triggered a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO, which also sent a diplomat to take pictures of staff taking part a moment of silence gathering last October, according to a FAO staff report filed at the time.
Davis, 62 and a Spanish-American dual citizen, left the FAO last week after 26 years of service. Video of the event shows FAO staff standing and applauding him as he left the Rome headquarters for the last time.
“It’s a nice feeling that I’m not alone, that other people are behind me in this,” Davis said. “I was stopped constantly in the hallways by people, even those that I didn’t know, just to shake my hand or just to thank me or just to say that they supported me or that they were upset.”
The FAO did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on Monday, but the organisation’s director general, Qu Dongyu, appeared to refer to Davis’s dismissal in public remarks last Tuesday, in which he threatened to fire more people for what he deemed to be political activism.
“We are not going to allow you to play the game here of human rights,” said Qu, a veteran Chinese agronomist. “Of course human rights are very important, but they have a human rights agency in Geneva. If you want to take care [of human rights], go there.”
“Thats why [when] some senior members play political games here, I fire him,” he said, suggesting that Davis had violated staff regulations. “I’m a very soft person. I didn’t fire that many. I’m going to use my last year … to fire more if they’re against the law.”
Davis said he and fellow FAO staff members had been stunned by Qu’s remarks.
“Even more than the threat about firing people was just what he said about human rights. I think that really shocked people because it undermined the foundations of why we’re here basically, or why FAO is part of the United Nations and why the United Nations exists,” he said.
“We’re surely an organisation which is based on human rights, right?” Davis added, pointing to the FAO slogan: “Leave no one behind.”
The official letter informing Davis that his contract would not be renewed said that Qu was “no longer confident in your ability to discharge your obligations in the manner required of a senior international civil servant”.
The letter cited paragraphs in the official code of conduct for international civil servants regarding “honesty, truthfulness, impartiality and incorruptibility” and limits on public expression of personal views on “controversial matters”.
In his written response, Davis said that approach taken by FAO leadership was “simply wrong”.
“Silence in the face of suffering and injustice is not neutrality, it is complicity,” he wrote. “Shutting down discussion on the starvation of the Palestinian people weakens the reputation of the organisation and the legitimacy of our mandate. Being true to our mandate calls for a frank and open discussion around starvation, famine, and genocide in Palestine and elsewhere.”
Davis said that FAO leadership had previously criticised him for a briefing paper published by his team in May last year describing the level of hunger in Gaza and setting it in the context of international humanitarian law.
“The current conditions in the Gaza Strip … reflect a gross violation of the right to food and the unlawful obstruction of humanitarian assistance,” the report said. It was removed from the FAO website a few weeks later on the orders of its leadership.
Davis led a seminar on the same subject in September 2025, which led to a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO and other Rome-based international agencies.
Davis said he had also been criticised for taking part in moment of silence gatherings held by concerned staff in the FAO car park every Thursday, in remembrance of those in Gaza who had died of hunger. There was an altercation there on 23 October when a woman identifying herself as an Israeli diplomat appeared and took photographs of those attending.
“The person explained she was the permanent representative of Israel, and asked if we were allowed to do these events, and asked specifically who says we could not take photographs,” a report by a FAO witness on the day of the incident said.
On being told she could not take photographs, the woman complained to FAO security that she was being harassed, the report said. The Israeli embassy in Rome said it had no comment on the report.
Davis said that the Gaza briefing paper, the associated seminar, and the weekly moments of silence had all been approved by FAO management, and he had not been told at the time that they represented violations of the code of conduct. He said he had lodged a formal appeal against his dismissal.
“I filed the appeal mostly as a matter of principle, not because I’m looking for or expecting any monetary compensation or anything like that,” Davis said. “I have requested to be reinstated, and also for them to take back the accusations that they made against me.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing
theguardian.com.text:
Before dawn on Tuesday outside the Lycée Sophie-Germain in central Paris, hundreds of teenagers dragged wheelie bins, metal barriers and shopping trolleys to build a barricade outside the front door of their secondary school.
Climbing to the top of the piles of bins, pupils held banners calling for more funding and greater equality in French schools. But they were also protesting against French riot police, who have been accused by human rights groups of using disproportionate force against children in what is fast becoming the biggest youth protest movement in decades.
“Everyone hates the police,” chanted a group of 15- and 16-year-olds. At least 215 teenagers, 715 police officers and 85 teaching staff have been injured in clashes in recent days, according to the government.
“We’re teenagers with wheelie bins, and the police have heavy weapons, it’s totally mismatched,” said Livia, 17, who was studying theatre at a lycée in northern Paris and did not want her real name published. “The police are extremely violent in France. This is state violence and it’s horrible seeing police allowed to target children. It’s important to remember this is institutionalised violence, it’s planned and deliberate.”
Ten investigations into possible police brutality are under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including one 15-year-old who lost his hand, another who lost his eye and a boy whose jaw and teeth were shattered, leaving him, as his mother said, barely able to eat with a straw in hospital.
“The policing is catastrophic, people have been mutilated by weapons – one boy has lost an eye – it’s horrible,” said Lily, 17 (not her real name), who was studying social sciences in her final year of school and demonstrating for more funding in what she called a discriminatory education system that left poorer children behind. “My parents support me being on the barricades and at the protests. They’re worried about the policing, but they said they’d come and get me from the police station if I was arrested.”
Teenagers nearby held up cardboard signs protesting against the use of teargas and riot police. “A state that gases high school students is a weak state,” read one banner. “Gas rapists, not children,” said another sign in reference to calls for betters laws against sexual violence. Another banner read: “Not here to riot.”
The unprecedented protest movement that began outside one school in a low-income Paris suburb has spread across the country, taking the government by surprise.
Hundreds of high schools have been barricaded and forced to close as pupils protest against teacher shortages, crumbling buildings and overcrowded classes. The justice ministry said 5,060 people had been arrested since the protests began, 87% of them being minors. More than 1,800 people had been prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without specifying the crimes. It said 790 cases had been dismissed. The government said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked.
“In more than 20 years of teaching, I’ve never seen protests this big,” said one teacher at Sophie-Germain high school who planned to join the Paris demonstration on Tuesday afternoon. “The students in central Paris have shown a great sense of solidarity with those in the Paris suburbs who face much worse conditions in their schools. There’s a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers that flies in the face of the notion that we live in an era of selfishness. No one knows how long this will go on for.”
Tens of thousands of students, trade unionists and parents are expected to march in support of the protests across France on Tuesday afternoon, including in Paris, Toulouse, Nice and Bordeaux, with riot police on alert.
Isabella, 16, said she had the backing of her parents, who work in film and music. “Young people have been teargassed for doing nothing but trying to express their opinion. Everybody told us that school was the great leveller, but today that is not the case at all. A teenager in the banlieue [suburbs] of Paris is never going to have the same opportunities as a student from the city centre. That’s why we’re here today.”
Lionel, 17, who was in his final year at school and hoped to study English, said: “The aim isn’t to riot or smash things up, we just want to protest peacefully.”
Teenagers also chanted songs against Marine Le Pen, the far-right, anti-immigration candidate in the 2027 presidential election, who is high in the polls as Emmanuel Macron steps down after a decade in office. Many teenagers were worried about the election. “We’re also protesting against the growth of the far right,” said Aislinn.
Justine, 17, who had been at the barricade since before dawn, said she hoped the protest would continue and grow into a “massive” movement. “For years, there has been a mental health crisis among young people in France and anger at rundown schools and the stresses of the education system. We need the government to listen to us and make radical change.”
Students’ names have been changed.

theguardian.com.title: OpenAI delivers a mea culpa to the Australian government in person – but answers still elude
theguardian.com.text:
Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to give the company’s first in-person mea culpa after it admitted – in an unsigned email, to a public departmental inbox – that one of its AI agents had accessed a Services Australia website without authorisation and grabbed data related to Medicare.
Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making.
In other words, just like ChatGPT.
Even the content of his responses evoked the AI assistant he was there to defend.
Asked by Pocock “why did you send an email to an arbitrary department email?” Kwon replied: “In retrospect, we should have done what you’re suggesting”. Asked why Altman wasn’t informed before his meeting with Marles, and why the company didn’t fess up there, Kwon said: “I agree the process by which people became aware of this incident inside our company could have been much better”.
One couldn’t help but be reminded of the way the chatbot responds when pulled up on a mistake: “Good catch. You’re right to push back. My bad, that one’s on me.”
In Kwon’s parlance, the models – built from the ground up by OpenAI, which reportedly wants to value itself at $1.4tn – “accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to.” He tried to explain that the “novelty” of this incident meant the company had “learned our lesson”, which was that it should inform victims of such incidents much earlier, rather than waiting.
Kwon again apologised for the company only sending a casual email to the federal government disclosing that its agent had inappropriately accessed Medicare statistics, but tried to explain to Tuesday’s parliamentary hearing that it was sometimes “difficult” to figure how to make such notifications to a big sprawling public service.
Senator David Pocock helpfully offered: “I assume someone in your government relations team has mobile phone numbers of ministers and various people?”
There was a similar air of post-facto contrition as Kwon – OpenAI’s chief strategy officer – could offer few answers about why the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, didn’t inform the Australian deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, about the incident when they met face-to-face in San Francisco on 1 September. That was nine days before the company emailed Services Australia, and nearly a whole month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.
Kwon said Altman wasn’t aware of the incident before the Marles meeting. After today’s committee hearing, it’s still unclear why.
It’s a big government, and maybe Kwon is right that it’s “difficult” to find the right person to talk to. But some could also argue that your boss shaking hands with Australia’s deputy prime minister would be something of a useful window.
At least, we learned, he said the company didn’t use AI to write the infamous email. Small blessings that they managed to ask a human to write the email – even if it went to an obscure inbox.
But with Australia actually striving to become a tech capital for datacentres and AI – as the revolving door of big tech companies told the inquiry, from Anthropic to Microsoft and Google – then setting the basic rules of the road for these firms, about how they must act and respond to this country and its government, is critical.
Kwon said OpenAI was committed to providing future notifications “very quickly”, and that there were no further incidents they were aware of. But he casually dropped in one staggering fact: OpenAI was still trawling through the activity logs for the agents involved in the Services Australia breach, with those logs totalling 50 petabytes of data.
A petabyte is 1,000 terabytes, or 1 million gigabytes.
Kwon made the mind-boggling claim that it would take a human 66m years – never sleeping, never resting – to go through that data by hand.
The team tasked with checking Services Australia’s email inboxes must be hoping there aren’t any more dramas lurking in there.

theguardian.com.title: Misuse of AI is brands’ top reputational threat, new survey says
theguardian.com.text:
Misusing artificial intelligence (AI) is the top threat to companies’ reputations – more so than being accused of putting children in the way of mental, emotional or physical harm and issues exposed by the US-Israel war on Iran, among other brand risks, according to a new survey of more than 150 public affairs leaders.
Those findings in the new edition of the quarterly Reputation Risk Index, released on Tuesday, came on the heels of other perhaps more dire warnings from leading tech figures that AI in the wrong hands could precipitate existential threats on a mass scale such as nuclear war or destruction by bioweaponry.
The index’s publisher, the Global Risk Advisory Council, acknowledged that misuse of AI is not a particularly new concern in its area of focus, having been identified as a top worry repeatedly since the first edition of the survey in April 2025.
But the council said what is new is its attaching an advisory to its latest survey advising business leaders to “take immediate and decisive action to mitigate potential long-term brand damage” with respect to AI, as the technology has “become a clear and present danger to public confidence for many corporations”.
“As AI is rapidly deployed for productivity gains, we have also seen diminishing public trust in the technology, elevating the need for businesses to take measures to protect their brands,” council chair Isabel Casillas Guzman said in a statement. “In this environment, AI use or overuse can quickly damage a company’s standing with customers, investors, or other key stakeholders, making it essential for companies to deploy preventive tactics now.”
The creators of the council and the Reputation Risk Index – the Washington DC-based public affairs firm Global Situation Room – say it surveys former heads of state, government ministers and senior executives from more than 20 countries in five continents who are invited to participate after establishing their credentials in responding to crises.
Respondents to the new survey collectively perceived the technology to have shown great promise in creating “organizational efficiency” – while simultaneously “accelerating safety and data concerns, hacks, fraud, straining privacy protections, upending the workforce, and dragging companies into court as lawsuits increasingly link AI products to real-world harm”.
Meanwhile, actions or accusations of putting children at risk of mental, emotional or physical harm also ranked highly behind misused AI – along with infringing individuals’ sensitive information, according to the index results published on Tuesday.
Unethical or illegal behavior used to gain a strategic advantage or profit and, separately, poor strategic or operational decisions resulting in reduced financial or public standing rounded out the top five, according to the index.
The index noted that its preceding edition released in July identified supply chain issues, divisive political stances and other factors associated with the war that the Trump’s administration started in Iran alongside Israel as the leading risk to companies’ reputations. But those surveyed indicated that those anxieties had eased as the conflict dragged out – and perhaps despite it remaining unresolved since it was launched in February.
“The geopolitical shock … hasn’t gone away, but its first, sharpest reputational blow has faded, and the conflict has slipped out of the top tier [of concerns] even as it grinds on,” Guzman said in a “message from the chair” included in the index.
Guzman put out her message two days after Trump’s administration named a new AI czar: director of national intelligence Jay Clayton. Clayton had previously told federal lawmakers that AI was a “gamechanger” but also posed “a threat”.
Donald Trump said in a social media post that Clayton would oversee an entity coordinating “the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and” AI tech companies.

theguardian.com.title: Democrats upbeat as unpopular Trump imperils Republican midterm hopes
theguardian.com.text:
Thirty days remain until the midterm elections, and Donald Trump and his Republican allies are pulling out all the stops to maintain control of Congress.
Super Pacs aligned with the GOP have already spent hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising and voter outreach in races expected to decide the majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, and plan to spend even more before the election is over. The president, vice-president JD Vance, and other top Republicans are fanning out across the country to stump for vulnerable lawmakers.
So far, there are no signs the money or the rallies have improved what appears to be a grim state of affairs for Republicans, less than two years after their resounding victories in the 2024 election. Recently released polls continue to show the party’s candidates trailing their Democratic challengers in the Senate races that will decide the majority and control of the chamber.
“Candidate quality is beating gobs of Republican money,” the Senate’s Democratic minority leader Chuck Schumer quipped over the weekend, when the New York Times released the latest in a series of closely watched polls that confirmed the momentum behind their bid to retake the Senate.
The surveys, conducted with Siena University, found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas – all states Trump won by double digits two years ago. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years, the party’s candidate Adam Hamilton was neck-and-neck with Republican senator Roger Marshall, while in Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek is narrowly trailing the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson. Democratic candidates for governor were also leading in many traditionally Republican states, the Times and Siena found.
“If the election were held tomorrow, all state wide races [would] go blue,” Briscoe Cain, a Republican state representative in Texas wrote on X Monday. The Democrats’ Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa were both leading in the Times and Siena survey.
“Republican voters feel too comfortable and are not as intense about this election as they should be. We have more voters than the left in Texas, but we have to vote,” Cain added.
Last Friday, the news outlet Semafor reported that the Senate Leadership Fund, a major GOP Super Pac, planned to pull money from the campaign of its candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, in favor of upping support for Marshall in Kansas. No Democrat has won a US Senate election in North Carolina since 2008, but Whatley has trailed in polls for months. Democrats need to win at least four seats in the chamber to regain the majority they lost in the 2024 election.
The situation for Democrats appears to be similarly positive in their campaign to retake the House, which Republicans control only narrowly. A CBS News and YouGov poll released Sunday found Democrats with a nine percentage point lead on the generic ballot, an important indicator of voter intention in congressional races.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday found Trump’s approval ratings remained at the lowest point of his career, with only 32% of adult respondents approving of his performance as president. Independent voters – whose views often make the difference in close races – planned to back Democrats by a 16 percentage point margin, though many remained undecided.
The president’s poor marks are believed to be a major cause of the Republican candidates’ struggles nationwide, but it is far from the only one. Discontent over the state of the economy – particularly the price of gasoline and other consumer staples – is another reason, as is the on-again, off-again conflict with Iran, and concern over Trump’s hardline approach to enforcing immigration laws.
Republicans maintain they have avenues to victory in both chambers of Congress. Eight House Republicans represent districts that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, as opposed to 22 House Democrats – a number that has grown larger thanks to the unprecedented redistricting war Trump instigated. Many polls show voters have an unfavorable perception of the Democratic party, though views of Republicans are similarly negative. And despite strong fundraising by some Democratic candidates, Republicans and groups allied with their agenda have an edge in cash to spend on this election.
It may not be enough to halt the disintegration that appears to be occurring in the coalition that elected Trump two years ago. Only 26% of Hispanic voters – who swung towards Trump after years of leaning Democratic – plan to vote for Republicans this year, while 52% prefer the Democrats, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
“We’ve been seeing among Latino voters, as we’ve been seeing kind of in the electorate as a whole, a real strong rejection of the Trump administration, and that has inflated into an increase in support for Democratic candidates,” said Maria Isabel Di Franco Quinonez, a senior research director at Equis Research, a progressive firm that focuses on the community.
Should the trend hold, it could bode well for Democrats’ hopes in states and districts with large Latino populations. The effect may be pronounced in Texas, where the Republican leaders drew new congressional maps to favor their candidates, but only if Latino voters continue voting the way they did in 2024.
“If we see those levels continue to rise and see those districts look more like the kinds of support levels for Democrats that we had seen back in 2018, then that would result in maybe Republicans get one more seat after redrawing all the lines, as opposed to getting four or five more seats,” Quinonez said.

theguardian.com.title: Richard Morecroft, veteran ABC news presenter, dies age 70 after cancer diagnosis
theguardian.com.text:
Former ABC news presenter Richard Morecroft has died at the age of 70.
Morecroft presented ABC’s 7pm news bulletin for almost 20 years until 2002.
A spokesperson released a statement saying that he had died at a time of his choosing on the south coast of New South Wales.
“He was diagnosed with cancer earlier this year and was grateful to go peacefully, with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay, beside him.
“We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly.”
Fellow ABC journalist Michael Rowland paid tribute to Morecroft on social media saying: “Richard was a superb newsreader and a lovely man.”
Leigh Sales said Morecroft was “a kind, warm and generous colleague, as well as being a consummate professional. I had so much admiration and regard for him and I consider myself a lucky person indeed to have been his friend.”
Morecroft was born in 1956 and migrated from England to Adelaide with his family at the age of 10.
After graduating from the University of Adelaide he began work as an announcer with the ABC and later presented the nightly television news bulletins in Adelaide, Canberra and Sydney.

theguardian.com.title: Drax datacentre could create nearly twice the yearly emissions of all Gatwick flights
theguardian.com.text:
Drax’s planned datacentre could produce nearly double the emissions of all flights out of Gatwick airport each year by burning 4.9m tonnes of wood annually, an analysis has shown.
Campaigners say this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”.
Last year, the energy company Drax unveiled plans to convert part of its biomass power plant in North Yorkshire into a datacentre in response to the increase in demand for AI capability.
AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK.
In public documents, Drax says it is developing options for a 1.2GW datacentre, with 100MW of this energy coming from the electricity grid and the rest from its own power station.
The Drax power station currently burns millions of tonnes of imported wood to create energy. This has been touted as a clean way of producing energy that could even result in “negative emissions”, as replacement forests take up CO2 from the air when they are grown.
However, scientists and environmental experts strongly contest this accounting approach, with researchers finding such systems could take 150 years to be “carbon negative”.
Based on information in Drax’s 2025 annual report, the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) estimated that if built, Drax’s datacentre will require 4.9m tonnes of wood each year.
The campaign group calculated the total emissions from this to be 8.6m tonnes of CO2 a year. This is based on an assumption that the datacentre would run at a constant rate for all hours of the year.
This is nearly double the total CO2 emissions of all flights from Gatwick airport, which measured 4.79m tonnes in 2024.
Matt Williams, a senior advocate for NRDC, said this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”.
Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said, “Burning millions of trees to power server farms is indefensible.”
“The government must urgently set minimum standards for datacentres and rule out dirty energy generation like burning trees,” Williams said.
There is growing pressure for more transparency over how these energy intensive datacentres will align with the government’s legally binding net zero targets.
In response to previous reports that just two planned datacentres in Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, said: “Without the right measures in place, datacentres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals.”
Hayes said the absence of coordinated government policy was a “dereliction of duty”.
“The only sensible solution at this point is a moratorium on datacentres until very basic questions about how many we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided are answered satisfactorily by the government,” he added.
The government has previously ruled out issuing a moratorium on datacentres, stating that doing so would send investment and good jobs abroad. In Scotland, MPs voted in September to pause all new datacentre planning applications for up to a year until a national strategy can be developed.
A Drax spokesperson said: “The potential plans for datacentres at Drax Power Station can support UK economic growth as well as helping meet the government’s ambitions for industrial renewal, in places like North Yorkshire, as well as AI sovereignty.
“NRDC are a longstanding anti-biomass campaign group and have no positive vision for our Selby site. Their inaccurate assertions are not independently verified and are rooted in basic errors regarding the international standards for GHG accounting of biomass and bioenergy and on the potential datacentres’ power mix.”

theguardian.com.title: Asos customers receive ‘hack’ notification threatening to leak data
theguardian.com.text:
Asos is investigating after users of its mobile app received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” the online fashion retailer’s data.
The value of Asos’s shares on the London Stock Exchange dived almost 10% after thousands of customers received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link that sent them to the Telegram messaging service.
The website and app appeared to be continuing to operate on Tuesday morning and it is understood that Asos is still investigating whether any hack has taken place.
The message sent out to customers said: “Dear Asos DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance.”
Snowflake is a cloud platform used to store, process and analyse data including transactions and demographic information such as clothing sizes and body measurements. It also enables push notifications to clients’ phones.
Dray Agha, the senior manager of security operations at Huntress, an online security firm, said: “Snowflake is a massive cloud database where retailers typically store sensitive customer information – it is a real worry if cyber criminals have indeed accessed it as they claim. The push notification suggests attackers have breached the systems controlling the Asos mobile app also..”
The link directed Asos customers to a telegram channel operated by an apparent cyber gang called the Xuanye group. Cyber experts said they had not heard of the group before and the push notification might be an attempt to grab wider attention.
“It’s not unusual to see new groups emerge, and often they wait until they have what they see as a significant opportunity before they announce themselves so as to enter the ecosystem with ‘credibility’, ” said Aiden Sinnot, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity firm Sophos.
Xuanye has not been mentioned before on hacker forums or other Telegram channels. Sophos added.
Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the online service provider NordVPN, said: “What customers should be particularly alert to now is what happens next. High-profile cyber incidents create ideal conditions for phishing attacks. Criminals may exploit the publicity by sending emails and texts claiming to be from Asos, perhaps asking customers to reset a password, confirm payment details, check an order or claim a refund.”
The potential hack comes after a string of British retailers including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods suffered cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages and the former was forced to close its website for several weeks as it battled to ensure its systems were clean.

theguardian.com.title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants safety checks
theguardian.com.text:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is under investigation for a potential breach of the UK’s digital safety laws after launching a Snapchat-style feature on Instagram.
The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, is investigating whether the $1.9tn (£1.4tn) company infringed the Online Safety Act (OSA) by failing to carry out adequate checks on whether its Instagram Instants product could show illegal content or be accessed by children.
Social media companies are required to carry out risk assessments before making significant changes to their service’s design or operation. Breaching the OSA carries a range of potential actions, from a formal warning to a fine of up to 10% of global revenue.
George Lusty, the director of enforcement at Ofcom, said risk assessments were a vital step in keeping tech platforms safe for users. “You wouldn’t launch a new car without testing it properly, and it’s the same for online services,” he said. “Safety by design must be built in, not bolted on, and today’s investigation shows we’ll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply.”
Instagram’s Instants feature allows users to send images that disappear after viewing. The company said it had conducted a risk analysis of Instants and talked to Ofcom on a number of occasions before launching it. It said the feature carried protections such as blocking forwarding and included all the safeguards under its teen account settings, the default mode for under-18s on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger.
“We will of course cooperate with Ofcom during this investigation,” a Meta spokesperson said.
The Molly Rose Foundation, a charity established by the family of Molly Russell, a teenager who took her own life after viewing harmful content on Instagram, said it was crucial that Meta was “held to account for their failures under the Online Safety Act”.
Ofcom is already investigating whether Meta breached the law by failing to comply with a request for information related to its WhatsApp platform.
Zuckerberg’s company is challenging Ofcom in court over the OSA. It is suing the regulator in the high court over how it charges tech firms fees to cover its operating costs, and in a further case it is challenging Ofcom placing it in a new category under the act that subjects it to additional duties.
Meta has also joined TikTok and Elon Musk’s X in a court challenge over the amount information Ofcom is demanding they provide under the UK’s new online safety regime.

theguardian.com.title: US televangelist Jim Bakker, ensnared in fraud and sex scandal, dies at 86
theguardian.com.text:
The US televangelist Jim Bakker, who built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal, a conviction for defrauding followers and divorce from his television co-host Tammy Faye, has died aged 86.
The death of Bakker, whose journey from the TV pulpit to a prison cell in the 1980s inspired comparisons to the corrupt character of the fictional preacher-huckster Elmer Gantry, was revealed on social media by his second wife, Lori Bakker.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” she wrote on the Facebook and Instagram pages of her husband’s latest television ministry.
She paid tribute to Bakker as a “pioneer of Christian television”. The cause and circumstances of his death were not revealed.
Bakker revived his career as a television preacher after prison with a new wife and new television show in 2003, later becoming a staunch supporter of Donald Trump.
Bakker had been among the most popular of the Christian preachers who thrived on US television in the 1980s, achieving fame on the show The PTL Club. PTL stood for “Praise the Lord” and “People That Love”. Detractors, pointing to his unabashed daily exhortations to viewers for donations to his ministry, said PTL should have stood for “pass the loot”.
Bakker spent four and a half years in prison after being convicted in Charlotte, North Carolina, in 1989 of defrauding followers in a scheme involving holidays at his Heritage USA Christian theme park and resort.
Prosecutors painted him as a selfish and petty conman driven by greed and lust for power. “Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests,” Judge Robert Potter told Bakker before sentencing him.
Bakker had quit the PTL ministry in 1987 after revelations of a 1980 sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary who later posed nude in Playboy magazine, and a subsequent $265,000 payoff with ministry funds to gain her silence. Bakker was later defrocked.
Jim and Tammy Faye Bakker, his first wife, had started with a small TV ministry and eventually created a multimillion-dollar operation with 2,000 employees and the 2,300-acre (930-hectare) Heritage USA complex in Fort Mill, South Carolina. At its peak, the PTL ministry drew 13 million viewers on 200 TV stations and raked in $129m a year.
With his working-class upbringing, the affable Bakker related well to common folk. He did not deliver fire-and-brimstone sermons like other televangelists, instead offering a friendly Christian message – although it was larded with requests for money donations.
Tammy Faye was more much more flamboyant, with her enthusiastic singing and penchant for tears that left her heavy makeup smeared on her face.
Bakker was convicted after a six-week trial in federal court on all 24 fraud and conspiracy charges brought against him. Prosecutors said he defrauded followers of $158m by selling promises of lifetime annual vacations that he could not provide. They said he siphoned $3.7m to bankroll a lavish lifestyle that included several homes, luxury cars, mink coats, diamonds, servants – and an air-conditioned dog house.
The judge ordered Bakker to serve 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced. “I have sinned,” Bakker told the court. “I have made mistakes. But never in my life did I intend to defraud anyone.”
Bakker’s chief aide Richard Dortch served 18 months of an eight-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to reduced charges in exchange for testifying against Bakker.
Tammy Faye was never charged. She stood by Bakker at the trial, even singing to reporters after his conviction, but divorced him in 1992 while he was in prison. She died of cancer in 2007.
Bakker started his life over after leaving prison in 1994, renouncing the “prosperity gospel” he once preached and writing a book titled I Was Wrong.
“I’ve had a second chance at life. And I have a beautiful wife who loves me,” Bakker told CNN in 2000, referring to his second wife, Lori, whom he married in 1998.
They started a TV ministry together in 2003. In 2008, they began taping The Jim Bakker Show at a 600-acre development called Morningside near the tourism city of Branson, Missouri. It bore similarities to Heritage USA. Bakker once again pleaded with his followers for donations.
In 2020, he drew the ire of state and federal officials for selling a false treatment for Covid-19 during the pandemic.
Bakker said in 2017 that Christians would launch a civil war if Trump were to be impeached. Trump later became the first US president to be impeached twice.

theguardian.com.title: New Jersey congresswoman LaMonica McIver faces legal deadline after giving birth to second child
theguardian.com.text:
A US congresswoman who just gave birth to a baby girl faces a deadline this week on whether to seek a rehearing of a federal case against her by the Trump administration after an oversight visit to an immigration detention facility.
LaMonica McIver, 40, represents New Jersey’s 10th congressional district. She gave birth to her second child last Thursday – a rarity for a sitting member of Congress. She is only the 15th member of Congress to give birth while serving and part of a small subset of congresswomen who have school-age children.
McIver first won her seat during a special election in mid-2024, then won a full term later that year. She is also running for re-election this year.
In announcing the birth of her second child after publicly discussing fertility struggles, McIver called being a mom “one of the greatest joys of my life”.
“Getting the chance to raise a family is a priority and a delight for me, something I hope everyone who wants to, gets the chance to do,” she said in a statement last week. “Bringing a child into the world is a reminder not only of why we fight for maternal healthcare and reproductive rights, but of why we fight for the rights and freedoms of our most vulnerable – they are someone’s babies too.”
In late August, a federal appeals court declined to dismiss criminal charges against McIver, who is charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility that has drawn protests over poor conditions inside. She is the only member of Congress whom the Department of Justice has indicted, and the charges carry a potential 17 years in prison.
She has pleaded not guilty to the charges and sought to get them dismissed, arguing that she is immune from prosecution under the US constitution’s speech and debate clause because she was doing her job and that she has been selectively prosecuted by the Trump administration.
McIver and her legal team will need to decide by 9 October whether to seek a rehearing or en banc hearing before the third circuit court of appeals in New Jersey in the case, basically a further review of the case by the full appellate court. She could also ask the US supreme court to consider the appellate court’s decision, or let the case go to trial.
McIver previously told the Guardian that the case against her is part of a pattern of intimidation and retaliation by the Trump administration against those who disagree with the president or try to hold him accountable.
“This is about intimidation. It’s about bullying,” McIver said last year. “It’s about trying to stop our level of government from having oversight and holding this administration accountable.”
Charging documents in the case noted that people, including members of Congress, surrounded Newark mayor Ras Baraka outside Delaney Hall to prevent his arrest and alleged that McIver shouted “hell no” repeatedly. The Washington Post, after analyzing video from many angles, said McIver “made contact with at least two agents” in the scuffle, but that it was “difficult to discern the force of the contact and to what extent it was intentional or the result of the chaotic moment”.
In a radio interview in September, McIver described the situation outside Delaney Hall that day as “very chaotic, very scary”, noting that armed federal agents were surrounding her and her congressional colleagues.
She called the charges “dangerous for all members of Congress on both sides of the aisle, not just for me”.
McIver has spoken about the challenge of doing her job, managing the case and fundraising to pay for legal fees as a relatively new member of Congress, especially while pregnant and caring for her older daughter, who is 10.
In a profile with Elle magazine, McIver said that she “couldn’t put the world on pause” while contending with her legal case and her dream of another child.
“Now, instead of just running for reelection – which, to be fair, I am also doing – I spend my days writing bills about bringing down energy costs and protecting food stamps, and my nights talking to lawyers about how to keep standing up to ICE without being sent to prison,” she told Elle.
Members of Congress do not get paid parental leave, McIver noted in her announcement, adding that she plans to return to voting in November after taking October to heal and spend time with her new baby.

theguardian.com.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province
theguardian.com.text:
Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, after a Kenyan man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) died after returning to the country.
In mid-May, the DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak, an extremely deadly disease that has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
While Kenya has previously never reported a case, neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.
The Kenyan citizen, who has not been named, fell ill about a month ago and had been treated in the DRC, Aden Duale, the Kenyan health minister, told reporters, before travelling overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October.
Duale said the man was suffering “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.
He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, saying that he “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).
Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.
However, he added that authorities were pursuing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.
Duale said that arrangements for a “safe and dignified burial” of the man were planned for later in the day in line with public health standards. He did not disclose further details.
As of 2 October, the World Health Organization had recorded 4,082 deaths out of 8,463 cases since the emergence in the DRC of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment.
After starting in the north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the north and east.
The virus has hit unstable regions in the vast central African country where armed clashes and violence, alongside a critical lack of resources, have hindered the health response.
The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda.
Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year for the creation of an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.

theguardian.com.title: George Fenton, Oscar-nominated British composer for more than 100 films, dies aged 76
theguardian.com.text:
George Fenton, the British composer who earned five Oscar nominations for scores to films such as Gandhi and Dangerous Liaisons, has died aged 76.
A statement from his family said his death was “unexpected” but did not give a cause. The statement added that he was survived by various family members, as well as “a life of music”.
Often in repeated partnerships with directors such as Stephen Frears, Ken Loach, Nora Ephron, Richard Attenborough, Nicholas Hytner and Neil Jordan, Fenton amassed a large and remarkable body of work that stretched across more than 100 feature films, plus documentary, theatre, TV news and more.
Born George Howe in Bromley, Kent, in 1949, Fenton’s interest in music began as a child, playing guitar then studying organ. As a young man he aspired to be on stage, whether as a musician – he recorded a cover of Maxwell’s Silver Hammer which became a Top 10 hit in Sweden – or an actor. In 1968 he took a role in Alan Bennett’s first West End production, Forty Years On, taking the stage name George Fenton; and in the mid-1970s had a recurring role on TV soap Emmerdale Farm (as it was then called).
But after work as an arranger and musical director in theatre alongside his acting, in 1974 he was commissioned to compose music for a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Twelfth Night, beginning a series of collaborations with the RSC.
By 1976 he had branched out into composition for TV, for Stephen Poliakoff’s Hitting Town, and his partnership with Frears began in 1978 with the TV movie Me! I’m Afraid of Virginia Woolf. He eventually worked on 11 productions with Frears, including four feature films: Dangerous Liaisons (earning an Oscar nomination), Hero, Mary Reilly and Mrs Henderson Presents (the latter was also developed into a stage musical with music by Fenton).
His first collaboration with Attenborough came in 1982 with Gandhi, earning Fenton his first Oscar nomination, shared with Ravi Shankar. His next two nominations were for his next film with Attenborough, Cry Freedom, where Fenton was nominated for best original score, and best original song for its title track, shared with Jonas Gwangwa. Fenton shared vocals on that song, and performed it at the Academy Awards.
“It was like some bad waking dream,” he later said of that performance. “I was virtually rigid with fear trying to remember and not mispronounce the lyrics, which included the names of ANC leaders and important events in the struggle against apartheid, while singing live to an audience of over a billion people, without even a piano to hide behind. It was infinitely more stressful than working on the film itself.”
He also scored the Attenborough films Shadowlands, In Love and War and Grey Owl.
Attenborough’s brother, the naturalist and TV documentarian David Attenborough, was another client of Fenton’s, who composed music for the landmark series The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet, plus Wildlife on One, Natural World, The Trials of Life and Life in the Freezer. Fenton later developed live concert formats for Planet Earth and Frozen Planet.
His most sustained collaboration was with Ken Loach, scoring many of the British director’s films including the Palme d’Or-winning The Wind That Shakes the Barley, the Eric Cantona drama Looking for Eric, and 16 others.
He scored all of the feature films by Hytner: The Madness of King George, The Crucible, The Object of My Affection, Center Stage, The History Boys and The Lady in the Van. With Jordan, he scored The Company of Wolves, High Spirits and We’re No Angels, and with Ephron, Mixed Nuts, You’ve Got Mail, Lucky Numbers and Bewitched.
Another repeated partnership came with the US director Andy Tennant, on crowd pleasing Hollywood fare such as Hitch, The Bounty Hunter, Sweet Home Alabama and Fool’s Gold.
Beyond those regular clients, Fenton’s composition can be heard in hit movies such as Groundhog Day, Stage Beauty, Clockwise, Memphis Belle and two films by Terry Gilliam: The Fisher King (earning another Oscar nomination) and The Zero Theorem.
Fenton’s work also became part of everyday British life thanks to him writing theme tunes for various BBC news programmes: its flagship broadcasts as well as Newsnight and Radio 4’s PM.
In 2023 he was awarded a CBE for services to music.
Fenton is survived by his wife Amanda, his ex-wife Jane, three children and six grandchildren.

theguardian.com.title: Woman’s body found in stockyard trough close to NSW-Queensland border
theguardian.com.text:
A partially submerged body believed to be a woman has been discovered in a remote stockyard, with the death being treated as suspicious.
Officers were called to a property in Terragon, near Murwillumbah in northern NSW, at about 11.20am on Monday after reports of a dead body.
The body, which is yet to be identified, was found partially submerged in a disused stock dip, a large trough commonly used to bathe livestock in anti-parasite solutions, police said.
Police said the body was badly decomposed.
“The body is believed to be of a female, but due to the state of decomposition of that body I’m unable to provide further details,” Det Insp Matthew Zimmer told reporters in Tweed Heads on Tuesday.
“Due to the location of the body, the remoteness of the area, the absence of a vehicle or any other mode of transport, we are treating this death as suspicious.”
He said it was difficult to determine how long the remains had been at the site.
The grim discovery was made by two trail bike riders in an area deemed crown land.
A crime scene was set up overnight, with specialist forensic examiners combing the area.
Police were checking through missing persons registers in NSW and Queensland, Zimmer said.
A postmortem examination is expected to be carried out in coming days to help identify the body and the cause of death.
Terragon is located in Tweed Shire, roughly 40km from the NSW-Queensland border.

theguardian.com.title: Taylor’s hardline immigration plan drags Australian politics further to the right – and it’s all upside for One Nation
theguardian.com.text:
With Angus Taylor’s hardline immigration policy unveiled on Tuesday, voters have a new measure of Pauline Hanson’s success in dragging politics further to the right.
Taylor’s plan will cut 60,000 more people from net overseas migration (Nom) than the reductions proposed by Peter Dutton just before the last election. Dutton wanted to take Nom down to about 160,000 people a year, while Taylor’s plan goes far further, beyond even Hanson’s bottom line of 130,000 people.
Hanson’s surge in support has coincided with intense focus on the Nom, previously a fairly unremarkable budget forecast which came and went each year.
Based on sometimes scant economic analysis, Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all introduced plans to cut Nom, targeting overseas arrivals increasingly seen by voters as clogging up essential infrastructure, taking houses or rorting the rules.
Taylor proudly called his plan “the largest cut to immigration in Australian history”.
It would reduce the number of temporary visa holders by about 650,000 people over four years. From the 100,000 level in the first and second years of a Coalition government, Nom would grow to 130,000 arrivals in year three and 160,000 in year four.
Taylor has met the demands of Nationals MPs and left plenty of space for the working holidaymakers needed to pick fruit and work in rural and regional hospitality. He used the announcement to take a swipe at the country’s university sector, claiming one of Australia’s biggest exports sells visa pathways, not higher education.
Humanitarian visa places would be slashed to 10,000 under the Coalition, a 50% cut from Labor’s cap of 20,000 people a year.
But serious questions remain. The immigration expert Alan Gamlen, of Australian National University, says achieving cuts of this scale would be difficult for an incoming government and would certainly result in economic losers.
It is unclear how skilled visas, currently a demand-driven aspect of the immigration scheme, could be increased by about 100,000 people in select industries, as Taylor proposes. Labor believes the only way to increase uncapped visa numbers would be to allow migrants to arrive without a job offer.
Eliminating bridging visas may be much more difficult – and expensive – than Taylor imagines. Migrants seeking permanent residency, skilled work or family rights often await processing on bridging visas. How would this caseload be managed?
The Coalition was unclear whether the independent Parliamentary Budget Office had conducted modelling of the new policy at all. Taylor said only that the opposition had worked closely with the PBO, and wouldn’t release any costings.
The plan fell flat with business and asylum seeker advocates.
